title: New hire handbook
description: Welcome to the product engineering group. Before your career clock starts, this handbook sets out the public rules. Everything in it is part of the published game design, and you can use it for long-term planning.

choices.action: Continue

title: In-house kernel versus an open-source stack
description: The company is setting up a new real-time compute platform, and your manager has put you in charge of the technology choice for your part of it. There are two options. You can build the kernel in-house, which fits the business but means a long build and a painful go-live. Or you can adopt a well-known open-source project, which lets you deliver quickly but leaves the kernel a black box and you at the mercy of upstream. The architecture review is next Friday and needs a decision.

choices.action: Argue for an in-house kernel as a long-term technical asset
Adopt the open-source stack and aim for fast delivery

title: Vaping at the neighbouring desk
description: After lunch, Robin at the next desk is vaping again. The cloud hangs over the open plan. The office rule is no vaping inside. You were hoping to concentrate this afternoon.

choices.action: Smile and quietly remind him vaping inside isn't allowed and the shelter is downstairs
Frown and put up with it without saying anything
Post a snide note in the channel: "some people might show a bit of consideration"

title: A colleague's late handovers keep pushing back your work
description: Your work cannot start until your colleague Will hands his over. He always delivers at the last minute. This time it arrives on the afternoon of the deadline, so you are stuck working late. He shrugs, "It was only a bit late."

choices.action: Agree a handover time with him, and bring in the project schedule if it needs writing down
Work late to cover it and say nothing
Call him out in the main channel as always holding things up

title: In-house kernel versus an open-source stack
description: The platform goes live on the open-source stack on time and the business is pleased. Then a routine security scan flags a problem: this version has an undisclosed candidate CVE, and details are already circulating among a few people internally. If it can be triggered in production, it would hit your core clients. The call is yours.

choices.action: Tell security and rush out a fallback from scratch
Sit on the report and bet it will not be triggered soon

title: Choosing a stack for a new module
description: You need to pick a stack for a new module. You could write the team's mature stack in your sleep, and it would almost certainly deliver on time. There is also a more modern framework with an active community that fits better in the long term. But neither you nor the team has used it in production, so expect pitfalls and an uncertain first release. The module is not on the critical path and the timetable is fairly generous. Your manager leaves the decision entirely to you. A proposal is due at next week's architecture huddle.

choices.action: Adopt the new framework and use this low-risk module to build experience
Stick with the mature stack and put reliable delivery first

title: Thanking a colleague from the next team who went out of their way
description: Last week a nasty bug in a barely maintained legacy submodule had you stuck for two days. Chris, a senior engineer on the next team, sat at your desk for a whole afternoon and helped you find and fix it. Nobody required them to spend that long. It is Friday, and you want to say thank you. You could take them out for a good lunch on you, around £30–40. You could write a formal recognition note on the intranet, copied to Chris and their manager, recording their high-quality cross-team help. Or you could do nothing special now and make a point of helping them next time they need it.

choices.action: Take them out for lunch privately, straight away
Write a formal recognition note and copy their manager
Do nothing special for now and help them next time they need it

title: A live demo blows up in front of the client
description: You are at the client's offices demonstrating a new feature. At the key checkout step the system throws an error and the page freezes. Their decision-makers sit opposite you, waiting to see it work. You know the demo environment is flaky, but the room has already gone cold.

choices.action: Say plainly it's a demo-environment glitch, and switch to a fallback or recording to show the core value
Keep hitting refresh as it gets messier, without switching plan
In a panic, say it is a problem on the client's network

title: Lunch with the team, or keep the break to yourself
description: At noon the team usually heads to a café near the office to swap project gossip and guesses about what your manager is thinking. It is where people pick up the unofficial news. For the past few months you have eaten at your desk or gone for a walk instead. You get a real break and are sharper in the afternoon. Colleagues have started calling you the lone wolf. At last week’s offsite your manager said you should mix with the team a bit more.

choices.action: Switch to lunching with colleagues at least three days a week
Keep skipping the café, and let a strong afternoon prove the point
Compromise: Tuesdays and Thursdays with the team, the break to yourself the rest

title: Lunch with the team, or keep the break to yourself
description: After a month of lunching with the team twice a week, your manager stops talking about “mixing in”. Over lunch you learn Warren’s project is being folded into your module, so you have time to prepare.

choices.action: Keep to the current pattern
Go to more lunches to stay more visible

title: Quarterly energy allocation
description: A new quarter begins and you have 3 Energy points. Unused Energy does not roll over. Plan your energy actions: you can combine several, as long as the total cost is no more than 3, and you can leave some or all of your Energy unused. The system applies each chosen action’s status_updates to your visible stats.

choices.action: High-intensity work
choices.description: Push hard on delivery. Output rises, Health and Dignity fall, and HiddenRisk goes up.

choices.action: Skill learning
choices.description: Spend time learning. Skill rises for the long run, but you are tired in the short term.

choices.action: Network maintenance
choices.description: Keep up relationships inside and outside the team. Network and Dignity rise slightly.

choices.action: Defuse legacy risk
choices.description: Clear up old problems before they bite. HiddenRisk goes down.

choices.action: Mental recovery
choices.description: Take time to reset. Dignity gets a solid boost.

choices.action: Health recovery
choices.description: Rest and recover. Health gets a solid boost.

choices.action: Prepare report materials
choices.description: Write up your visible wins early. Output and Dignity rise a little.

choices.action: Reserve energy (no action)
choices.description: Leave the rest of your Energy unused this quarter. It does not roll over.

title: Quarterly main action
description: This quarter you may pick one main action towards your career goals, or none. Each main action changes your stats straight away. Choose based on your visible stats, the promotion windows and your long-term plan. The system applies the chosen action’s status_updates.

choices.action: Apply for a key project
choices.description: Join a high-profile project. Output, Skill and Network all rise.

choices.action: Report results to your manager
choices.description: Tell leadership about your wins. You become more visible and better recognised.

choices.action: Fight for resources
choices.description: Push for budget, headcount, or support for your work.

choices.action: Apply for rotation
choices.description: Rotate into another team to broaden your skills. Skill rises strongly.

choices.action: Showcase results
choices.description: Present your results to a wider audience. Output and Dignity rise.

choices.action: Build a mentorship
choices.description: Work with a senior mentor. Network and Skill improve.

choices.action: Repair a key relationship
choices.description: Mend a strained relationship. Network and Dignity recover.

choices.action: Lay low and reduce risk
choices.description: Keep your head down. Health recovers and HiddenRisk falls.

choices.action: No action
choices.description: Skip the main action this quarter. Your stats do not change.

title: Client makes an inappropriate joke at dinner
description: You are at a client dinner. After a few drinks, one of their senior people starts making jokes that cross a line — pointed, sexual remarks aimed at Chloe, a woman on your side of the table. Her laugh is tight and she looks trapped. They are an important account. Everyone else is pretending it is banter. The table is waiting to see what you do.

choices.action: Change the subject without a scene, pull the talk back to the work, and give Chloe a way out
Join in and laugh along, to keep the ‘atmosphere’
Say firmly that the remark is not on, and bring the talk back to the work

title: The gym after work, or staying late to get ahead
description: You started going to the gym after work and have kept it up. You feel better and have more energy. Tonight there is a non-urgent piece of work that would make tomorrow easier if you finished it. You can only do one: the gym or staying late.

choices.action: Go to the gym as planned and get the work done efficiently tomorrow
Skip the gym, stay late, and clear the work tonight
Try to do both: gym first, then stay up late to finish the work

title: A live demo blows up in front of the client
description: You switch to the fallback without fuss, finish the core flow, and use it to talk through the system's fault-tolerance. The client even thinks you were well prepared. After the demo their engineering lead asks you privately what caused the error.

choices.action: Give the root cause straight, and promise a write-up of the investigation and fix afterwards
Fudge it: 'Small issue, doesn't affect anything'

title: A chatty, skiving colleague eating into your time
description: Luke, a teammate, has taken to hovering at your desk for half-hour chats: gossip, moaning, memes. You can tell their own workload is light and they mostly want someone to skive with. You have a critical module due for QA today and have already been interrupted three times. You need to decide how to handle it.

choices.action: Tell them directly but politely that you need to focus today and to come back later
Put headphones on, look busy, and give them the cold shoulder
Chat for a few minutes, then steer back to work and mention today's deadline
Tell your manager that Luke keeps breaking your concentration

title: Escape room: your manager is slowing you down, a quiet colleague is flying
description: Company escape room: The 1948 Files. Chris, your manager, insists on directing and is all over the place, retrying the same wrong codes. Quinn, usually quiet in testing, has just solved three puzzles in a row. Fifteen minutes left, one lock from the exit, and Chris is about to guess again.

choices.action: Ask Quinn to take the lock, and tell Chris: “You keep the big picture”
Say outright that Chris’s approach is wrong
Follow Chris’s guesses so he is not made to look small

title: A chatty, skiving colleague eating into your time
description: Luke takes a hint, but in the afternoon they bring snacks and want to "eat and chat". Today's QA deadline is still closing in.

choices.action: Turn down the snack session firmly and suggest lunch another day
Give in, chat for a quarter of an hour, and catch up in the evening

title: After dinner, karaoke with someone on the promotion panel
description: The Lynx team dinner is over. Helen, the HR business partner, who sits on the promotion committee, suggests going on to karaoke. You have a headache and want to go home. Nine people have already signed up in the channel, and only you and Lee have not. Helen tags you: “Come on — no work talk, just singing.”

choices.action: Go to the karaoke bar, keep your drinking in check, and join in
Decline politely and make sure you are sharp at the morning stand-up
Show your face for half an hour, then leave

title: Client makes an inappropriate joke at dinner
description: You steer the conversation onto the project and give Chloe an easy exit — a ‘call she needs to take.’ The client does not clock that you defused it, and the table settles. Afterwards Chloe thanks you privately. You still have to decide whether the company should know this client has a problem with boundaries.

choices.action: Brief your manager privately and factually, ask Chloe what support she wants, and raise it with the account lead
Decide it was handled and there is no need to raise it

title: A new colleague with no sense of privacy
description: Lou has just joined and is over-familiar from the start. Within days she has asked whether you own or rent, whether you are seeing anyone and how you get on with your manager. At lunch she also presses you on 'who on the team doesn't get on'. She means no harm and just doesn't seem to know where the line is, but the questions make you uncomfortable, and people nearby look awkward too.

choices.action: Laugh it off and gently draw a line: 'Let's not go there. Talk about something else?'
Be blunt: 'That's private. Please don't ask'
Answer each question, not wanting to embarrass a new colleague

title: A colleague's clutter takes over the aisle
description: Leon, who sits next to you, hoards things. Boxes, parcels and gym kit are all over the floor and have slowly taken over the shared aisle between you. You have to turn sideways to get past, and it is a trip hazard. He doesn't seem to see a problem.

choices.action: Tell him the aisle is too tight and suggest sorting the clutter together
Squeeze past every day and say nothing
While he is away, pile all of it onto his desk

title: A colleague keeps @channel-ing questions already answered in the docs
description: In the main project channel, new joiner Tessa @channels questions several times a day that are clearly in the docs or a thirty-second search away. Plenty of people are tired of the pings. This time it's a question answered on the first page of the wiki.

choices.action: DM her a doc link and suggest checking the wiki or asking the owner before using @channel
Call Tessa out in the channel: "Could you read the docs before asking?"
Ignore it like everyone else and leave the question hanging

title: A drunk colleague at the Christmas party
description: A few rounds into the Christmas party, Will, usually quiet, is loudly tearing into the department and is close to marching off to ‘have it out’ with your manager. Nobody else can get through to him. He is a decent person having a bad night. If this continues he will hate himself in the morning, and the scene will be ugly. You are standing closest.

choices.action: Steer him out, half-coaxing, half-supporting, and get him home with someone to look after him
Stay and watch, joining the crowd treating it as entertainment
Get well away so none of it lands on you, and leave him to it

title: A colleague keeps helping themselves to your snacks
description: You keep a few snacks in your drawer. Colleague Mia "just grabs a handful" every day, never brings her own, and has never returned the favour. Today she grins, "Yours are the best." It isn't much, but it is starting to grate.

choices.action: Joke: "Bring some next time and we can swap", and leave it there
Keep sharing, because you don't like to say anything
Lock the snacks away and stop sharing, without explaining

title: Late-night work messages and the manager's reaction
description: Colleague Tara posts "today's progress" and "tomorrow's plan" in the channel every night at 11pm. Your manager, Chris, is often first to react. You are never online at that hour. In the weekly meeting Chris said "we need to respond promptly". Tonight Tara @channels a question about an API field.

choices.action: Reply at once to look professional
Reply in the morning and spell out your working hours
Suggest to your manager privately that important items go by email
Copy Tara and start sending late-night updates yourself

title: Named on a department award you did not work on
description: Submissions for the department’s annual Breakthrough Award close tonight. Your manager sends you the Aurora data-platform pack to look over. You have been on Lynx Payments the whole time. The team next door delivered Aurora, and you only turned up to the kick-off. Your manager messages: “I’ve added you to the list to make the bench look stronger for the panel. Just sign it.”

choices.action: Ask that the pack name only those who did the work, or limit your line to the kick-off
Sign it quietly and treat it as a favour from your manager
Suggest submitting Lynx Payments instead, with you as the lead author

title: A new colleague with no sense of privacy
description: Lou picks up on it, looks a bit embarrassed and stops. You move the conversation on to work and hobbies, and things feel normal again. A couple of days later she is asking about 'team gossip' again. She really does not seem to know where the line is.

choices.action: Kindly suggest she gossips less and focuses on the work while she's new, for her own sake
Keep deflecting without spelling it out, and stay out of it

title: A senior puts their name on an intern’s work
description: During an Aurora reporting sprint, senior engineer Rowan puts the SQL work and visualisation templates of Quinn, the intern, into the weekly update under his own name. Quinn is listed as having “assisted”. Quinn comes to you in tears, too scared to take on Rowan, who trained with your manager. The review slides are finalised tomorrow.

choices.action: Name Quinn’s specific contribution in the meeting that finalises the slides
Ask Rowan privately to correct the credit
Tell Quinn to take it to your manager themselves
Stay out of it to avoid annoying Rowan

title: A senior puts their name on an intern’s work
description: Rowan says “it’s team output, we don’t divide it,” and refuses to change it. Quinn looks at you, disappointed.

choices.action: Send the weekly update and the git history to your manager
Drop it

title: A drunk colleague at the Christmas party
description: You get Will out before he does it in front of your manager. He is sick in the cab and, before he blacks out, mumbles a thanks. The next day he is mortified, and asks privately whether he made a scene and whether anyone senior saw.

choices.action: Tell him the truth: it never reached your manager, and suggest he watch his drinking next time
Turn it into a story and tell it round the office in full colour

title: Raising a technical objection on another team's API design
description: While reviewing a downstream API design from a neighbouring team, your own load tests flag a likely bottleneck: at peak, once QPS doubles, tail latency could jump from 50ms to around 800ms and threaten your SLA. Their design has already passed their internal review. The owner is a well-regarded senior engineer. Formal integration starts next Wednesday, so there is little time to talk it through. How you raise it will decide whether the design actually changes.

choices.action: Comment publicly on the shared design doc, with the load-test data attached
Take their owner aside for a 1:1 and walk through the load-test results privately

title: A colleague who keeps handing you his work
description: Dave on your team is very good at 'finding help'. One day it is two slides to rewrite, the next a script to run, and it is always 'you're better at this, it'll take minutes'. At first you were happy to help. Then you noticed more and more of his actual job coming your way as a matter of course, while he leaves early. Today there is another message: 'Mate, can you tidy this data? I've got to shoot off at five.'

choices.action: Help this time, and be clear: next time he drafts it first and you review
Decline gently: 'I'm swamped. You start it and I'll jump in if you're stuck'
Quietly take it on again so as not to sour the relationship

title: Raising a technical objection on another team's API design
description: Both teams see your comment. Their owner replies: "Thanks for the data — there is a risk, but the timetable is tight. Let's ship as designed and watch it in a canary." Your manager also tags you: "Be careful how you raise things in public. They have a reputation to protect." You need to decide whether to keep pushing for a fix before go-live.

choices.action: Insist on a pre-launch fix and attach a complete proposed patch
Accept the canary plan and add monitoring and a rollback playbook

title: A colleague who comes in ill
description: Faye at the next desk has a heavy cold. She is coughing constantly and has almost lost her voice, but she is still in: 'The milestone's tight, I can't drop the ball.' The whole open-plan floor can hear every cough, and two people have started sneezing. She sees it as doing her duty, but there is a real risk she will pass it on. You are on the same project.

choices.action: Check in privately, ask her to go home, and offer to cover the urgent part
Tell your manager her coming in ill is a health risk, and suggest sick leave while the team covers
Put on a mask, move away from the noise and the germs, and say nothing

title: Hosting an important client visit
description: An important client's head of engineering is visiting next week. Facilities has left the final plan to you, since you own the technical side of the partnership and will run the demo. There are three options. (A) Use the standard BD budget, drinks within policy included, for a working dinner at a nearby business restaurant, where you stay for two hours. (B) A working lunch in the office café, then an afternoon demo that covers the whole proposal in one sitting, with no evening meal. (C) A fully remote demo with no visit. All three are within policy. They differ in how much of your time and energy they take, and how warm the relationship feels.

choices.action: A: Working dinner at a business restaurant, staying two hours
B: Working lunch in the office café, then an afternoon demo covering everything in one go
C: Fully remote demo, no in-person visit

title: Telling the client the project will be late
description: An upstream dependency has failed on a project you own. You now know you will be a week late, and the original delivery date is three days away. The client cares a lot about this one and has even put their own name behind it internally. You need to decide how to tell them.

choices.action: Tell them at once, with a cause analysis, a recovery plan and a new timetable
Wait until delivery day in case you still make it
Report 'on time', then quietly work late and try to catch up

title: An unpublished restructure, and a friend about to buy a flat
description: You were copied on a restricted leadership note: a draft Q2 reorganisation. Lynx may be folded into Falcon Recs, with about 15% fewer roles. Nothing has been announced. Over dinner last night your friend and colleague Sienna said she wants to put in an offer on a flat, with the deposit already saved, and asked: “Is your team stable? I’m about to sign.” Her mother is ill and she needs the place.

choices.action: Hint that things may move soon and she should be careful, without naming the document
Say you cannot comment on internal plans or promise that any role is safe, so she must weigh the risk herself
Tell her privately what is planned and ask her to keep it strictly confidential

title: A collaborator shifts the blame in a meeting
description: You and Chloe share delivery on a client project. In the weekly meeting the client complains about repeated API changes and thin test coverage. Chloe speaks first: “The API design was mainly theirs. I worked to the version they gave me. Testing was held up on their team too.” In fact the changes came from the client changing their mind three times, and you emailed several times for a test environment without getting one. Your manager and the client both look at you. You need to respond in the room.

choices.action: Walk through the timeline and the email trail, and set out who owned what
Take some of the blame for now to steady the client, and leave Chloe for later
Hit back in the room: Chloe did not provide the integration environment on time
Stay silent and ask your manager to unpick it

title: A colleague who keeps handing you his work
description: You helped and said your piece. Dave agreed, then 'forgot' the next time and dumped the work on you again. In front of your manager he breezily called it 'something we always do together', blurring who did what. You realise a spoken agreement means nothing to him.

choices.action: Record what you help with in messages and ticket notes so credit is traceable, and reset the split
Leave it. It's less hassle to keep helping

title: A collaborator shifts the blame in a meeting
description: The emails show the client and your manager exactly how the changes came about. Chloe looks grim. Afterwards your manager tells you and Chloe to “sort it between yourselves”. The client wants a joint improvement plan this week.

choices.action: Draft a joint improvement plan, copy your manager, and invite Chloe to co-author it
Write only your own part and make clear where it ends

title: Whether to join a cross-team architecture review — and how hard to push
description: The department tech committee is holding a cross-team architecture review next week, covering next-quarter rebuilds of several core services. Reviewers get a vote and share responsibility for the outcome later. You have been invited as a cross-team reviewer (you have a lot of experience with API performance and reliability). Accepting means three or four days reading their design docs and preparing comments. If you decline, they review it among themselves. You miss a chance at cross-team influence, but your own timetable is untouched.

choices.action: Accept, read the docs properly, and prepare comments
Decline and keep the time for your own team's delivery

title: A colleague who comes in ill
description: Faye is touched but still hesitates: 'I feel bad, you've got your own work.' You take the most urgent part and she goes home. Now your own schedule is packed, the milestone is close, and you are feeling the strain.

choices.action: Tell your manager you are covering Faye for now, and ask for a realistic plan
Carry all of it without telling anyone, and work late to catch up

title: Telling the client the project will be late
description: You were straight with them early. The client is not pleased, but respects that you were professional and took responsibility: 'At least you didn't hide it. I can explain that internally.' Then they push: could you ship a usable core first and the rest next week?

choices.action: Check what is feasible, then offer phased delivery: the core first, the rest after
To keep them happy, promise both the core and the full version by the original date

title: Whether to join a cross-team architecture review — and how hard to push
description: You go in deep and raise a core objection to one design: they plan to introduce a framework that has not been used at scale inside the company, which carries a maintenance risk. Their owner disagrees in the meeting, fairly bluntly. The chair suggests you carry on the discussion afterwards. You need to decide what to do next.

choices.action: Write a full risk assessment and submit it formally to the tech committee
Defer to their judgement and file your comments as an appendix

title: A former colleague asks you for internal company material
description: A former colleague gets in touch, very friendly, and asks a "small favour": send them some internal material or data. "You've got it to hand. It's not a big deal." The material is company property and covered by confidentiality. What do you do?

choices.action: Decline, explain it is confidential company property that can't go outside, and keep things civil
Send the internal material because you feel you can't say no
Send it, plus extra they didn't ask for, to look generous

title: A newly hired VP talks to you alone for ten minutes on day one
description: Hale, a newly hired group VP, tours the Lynx floor, stops at your desk and asks how the payments circuit breaker works. You talk for ten minutes. Afterwards colleagues mutter about whether your manager is being replaced and whether you are about to shoot up the ladder. Tara turns polite and distant. Chris is suddenly unusually courteous to you.

choices.action: Brief Chris on Hale's questions and your answers
Don't make a fuss, and keep delivering as normal
Quietly take Hale's team out to lunch to build on the impression

title: You overhear a redundancy list that includes a friend
description: From a toilet cubicle you hear a VP and the HR director discussing the Q2 redundancy list: “…Ethan is in the consultation pool after the Lynx Wallet incident, package would be a standard redundancy…” Ethan is your tennis partner and helped you move last week. They wash their hands and leave, unaware you were there. The list has not been announced.

choices.action: Tell no one and act as if you never heard it
Hint that Ethan should keep his head down and not resign in a hurry
Tell him he is on the list and what the package looks like
Tell Ethan only about the published redundancy process and support channels, and nothing you overheard

title: A newly hired VP talks to you alone for ten minutes on day one
description: Two weeks later Hale does not follow up one-to-one. The gossip cools. Chris is back to normal.

choices.action: Let your project results strengthen your position
Moan that it was a nine-day wonder

title: The client adds three things 'while we're here'
description: Close to delivery, at a regular meeting, the client 'mentions in passing' three new requirements: 'These shouldn't be hard. Just do them at the same time.' In fact the change is a big one. It would squeeze the current plan and hurt quality. Their tone is casual, as if it is obviously included. Everyone in the room is watching how you respond.

choices.action: Neither accept nor refuse in the meeting, and promise an impact assessment and proposal afterwards
Afraid of annoying them, agree to all of it on the spot
Refuse there and then: 'It's not in the contract. We can't do it'

title: In-house senior architect certification over the weekend
description: The tech committee is running an in-house senior architect certification this Saturday and Sunday, on your own time. It is optional, and the company covers the fee. Meanwhile, an internal tooling project of yours is due next Tuesday as planned. If you put in extra hours this weekend, you could ship it on Monday morning, which your client contact says would save them a day of integration. You had already planned a weekend away with family. You cannot do all three. How do you spend the weekend?

choices.action: Sign up for the certification and spend both days learning properly
Work through the weekend to deliver the project on Monday morning
Stick to the family weekend and pick work up next week as planned

title: Where personal use of work kit stops
description: The company issues a high-spec workstation and a 4K display. Policy allows 'limited personal use' without saying exactly where the limit is. You have started using the work kit for a personal open-source project that does not compete with the business, and at weekends it soaks up a fair amount of compute. A colleague spots weekend commits from the office IP and jokes, 'So the company is sponsoring your open source now?' You realise it could be misread.

choices.action: Stop using work kit for the personal project immediately, and move it onto your own machines
Ask your manager and compliance whether the current use sits inside policy, and get it in writing

title: The client adds three things 'while we're here'
description: You assessed it properly afterwards. One of the three is small, but the other two would push the date back a long way. You have a table of impact, cost and schedule ready. The client is chasing for an answer.

choices.action: Talk numbers: do the small one for free, and put the other two through change control with plan trade-offs
Still dreading the conversation after the assessment, cram all of it into the current plan

title: You overhear an unpublished project naming you
description: In the fifteenth-floor kitchen, platform director Harper and Miles, a fellow manager, drop their voices: “Polaris starts in Q3. On the Lynx side we’ll have… lead the tech.” The word you half-catch in the gap is your surname. The project has not been announced. If Miles realises you were listening, it may look like you were fishing.

choices.action: Walk in as if you have just come for water and say hello as normal
Leave quietly and act as if you heard nothing
Stay in the corner and listen to the rest

title: A manager-free channel shares a screenshot of your boss
description: In the Lynx late-night Slack channel, where no managers are allowed, someone posts a screenshot of Chris tearing into people: "If you can't even do this, what bonus do you think you deserve?" The next message: "Thoughts? Should we reply as a group?" You're in the channel. Passing a copy to HR, a staff representative, a union or a solicitor so they can deal with the complaint is not itself a disciplinary matter. Spreading it to people who have nothing to do with the complaint is another matter.

choices.action: Ask them to stop spreading it, keep the evidence the target needs, and raise it through a grievance or staff rep
Join in and have a moan
Leave the channel and stay out of it
Message Chris privately about team morale, without saying how you know

title: A project you wanted going to someone else
description: You are running a live project that needs your full attention. The timetable is tight, and you own the fallout if it goes wrong. Your manager has just started a new project you have wanted for a while, with a new framework and external visibility, but the slot went to your teammate Owen. Your manager bumps into you in the corridor: “Stabilise what you're on first. I don't want you split across the new work this time.” You need to decide how to respond.

choices.action: Accept the plan and give the live project your full attention
Ask your manager if you can join the new project part-time
Approach Owen privately: you supply the technical design, they stay the lead

title: Pushed on stage at the Christmas party
description: The Christmas party is in full swing. The host spots you, and your table, colleagues and manager included, starts chanting for you to get up and do something to “get the room going.” You have nothing prepared and this is not your sort of thing, but every eye is on you and someone is already holding out a microphone.

choices.action: Take it in good humour: a quick gag or a bit of audience interaction, just enough to lift the room
Smile and say, ‘Thanks, but not tonight’
Shut it down flat with “I’m not doing that”, and let the room go quiet

title: Remote client keeps sending the work back
description: You are working with a remote client entirely over video and chat. After the first delivery they say on a call, “This isn’t what I wanted.” Your chat history shows they had informally agreed to that direction. Reworking it will be expensive, and the team is already grumbling. Their tone on the call is getting sharp.

choices.action: Skip the blame game: work out the mismatch and propose prototypes or visual specs before building more
Pull up the chat log and argue that they already confirmed it
Rework the lot without question, doing whatever they say

title: An engagement survey that asks for your staff ID
description: The annual engagement survey says answers are confidential. The portal asks for your staff ID and an SMS code, which may only be there to stop someone submitting twice. The page does not say whether anyone can later trace an answer back to you. You have a long list on Chris, your manager: goalposts that move, taking credit, weekend pings. A colleague believes that last year someone who wrote something sharp was frozen out afterwards.

choices.action: Fill it in honestly, with examples and no swearing
Score everything as blandly positive
Set out the moving goalposts, the credit-taking and the weekend messages as plain facts, without insults

title: A project you wanted going to someone else
description: Owen agrees on the surface (“let's do it together”), but in updates outside the team they mostly put their own name on the work. Your manager praises Owen in the channel for “pushing the new direction hard”. You need to decide what to do next.

choices.action: Clarify your actual contribution and what you want with your manager
Drop it and go back to focusing on the live project

title: A leaver asks you to keep work files off the company systems
description: One evening Felix, who is leaving for a competitor, sends you a link to 8GB of files in cloud storage: “Three years of project scripts and client-contact notes. I wiped the company drive — keep this for me, and don’t upload it here.” Some of the files are scanned client contracts marked Internal. You know his leaver agreement says he must not take business data with him.

choices.action: Refuse the files and tell him to use the proper handover
Take the link without opening it, and plan to delete it later
Take it and report it to Information Security

title: Pushed on stage at the Christmas party
description: You stay off the stage and at your table, chatting and clapping along. You are still very much part of the evening. Then the table turns on Jordan, a new joiner who hates this sort of thing, and they go bright red.

choices.action: Get Jordan off the hook: steer the attention elsewhere and give them a way out
Leave them to deal with it

title: One umbrella, a downpour, and Jordan at going-home time
description: A release ran late and you are finally leaving. Rain is hammering the glass and the Met Office has an amber warning out. In your drawer is a single folding umbrella you picked up from a hotel on a previous trip. Jordan, a teammate, has just stood up too, with no umbrella, and is staring towards the lobby. They live two stops from you on the same line. Cabs are a forty-minute wait. You need to decide how you get home.

choices.action: Offer to share the umbrella and walk to the station together
Lend Jordan the umbrella and make a dash through the rain for a cab
Suggest sharing a cab and splitting the fare
Say the umbrella only covers one, so you will each make your own way

title: Remote client keeps sending the work back
description: You suggest that from now on every requirement goes through a rough prototype and written sign-off. The client agrees: “That would actually make this much clearer.” You also agree a sensible scope for the first rework. The team still worries that endless changes will wreck the timeline and morale.

choices.action: Build sign-off and a change log into the process to protect both the client and the team
Fix how you communicate, ignore the timeline, and just work longer hours

title: One umbrella, a downpour, and Jordan at going-home time
description: The umbrella is small and your shoulders still get wet. On the way Jordan talks about your manager squeezing the timetable lately, and they sound low. At the station they hesitate: “Want to grab a bowl of something hot near mine? On me.” The rain is getting heavier.

choices.action: Accept, and listen to how the project is going
Decline and catch the last train home

title: Neck pain with a deadline — whether to keep the physio appointment
description: A stretch of late nights has left your neck aching and your right hand tingling. Physio is booked for tomorrow afternoon, which is also when a delivery checkpoint falls.

choices.action: Keep the physio appointment and shift delivery by half a day
Move the appointment to the weekend and push through delivery first
Stick on a heat patch, tough it out, and leave physio for later

title: You notice promotions going to the people who play politics
description: You have watched this for three years. The fastest riser is Harvey: average technically, but he never misses karaoke, five-a-side or the pub after work. Your technical scores have topped the team for years, yet your promotion still lags. Chris says they also look at “the whole picture”.

choices.action: Make more effort socially, without crossing your own lines
Refuse to play along and double down on technical output
Tell Helen, the HR business partner, that the promotion criteria are too vague
Start looking elsewhere and ease off here

title: A colleague hogging the printer
description: You need a short meeting pack printed now. Quentin is using the shared printer for a hundred-odd pages of personal material, checking each page as it comes out, with no sign of letting anyone in. You are short of time.

choices.action: Explain politely that you have something urgent and ask to jump in for two pages
Walk over, cancel his job and print yours first
Wait in silence while the meeting starts without you

title: A merge conflict wrecks release day
description: On release day you are merging the release branch. After a long session resolving conflicts, you accidentally pull in untested feature-branch code. CI is green because a flaky test skipped one check.

choices.action: Halt the release as soon as you notice and roll the merge back
Carry on with the release and gamble that the code path will not be hit
Quietly hotfix the wrongly merged files out

title: The company tries to keep you after you look elsewhere
description: You have been unhappy and have quietly thought about looking for another job, and it has started to show in how you talk. Your manager notices, takes it seriously and comes back with a retention package: a rise, a project, even a hint that you would be first in line at the next promotion round. Your doubts start to fade. You have to decide how to answer.

choices.action: Go back to why you wanted to leave, and only stay if the package actually fixes that
Let the rise decide it, and drop the idea of leaving on the spot
Say you will stay, and keep looking on the quiet

title: You notice promotions going to the people who play politics
description: The CTO sees your talk at a tech conference and moves you into architecture, bypassing Chris's reporting line.

choices.action: Take the move
Stay on the Lynx team

title: A junior asks to pair on your state machine
description: Intern Alex asks for two hours this afternoon to pair, so he can understand a state machine you wrote. You have a bug that needs to be fixed by four.

choices.action: Reschedule: pair first, then fix the bug
Point him at the docs and comments and let him work through it
Pair for an hour and do the rest asynchronously

title: Whether to warn that the sprint is overcommitted
description: In sprint planning, Product brings in far more story points than the team can handle. Your manager looks at you: “Can we do it?” Everyone else stays quiet.

choices.action: Use the numbers to show the team is over capacity, and suggest cutting scope
Nod and take it on
Raise it privately with your manager after the meeting

title: Should you leave the company a bad Glassdoor review?
description: You have a stack of grievances and fancy leaving a low score and a rant on Glassdoor, as a warning for the next person and a chance to get it off your chest.

choices.action: If you write, stick to facts: no exaggeration, no confidential detail, no personal attacks
Write a long, emotional recap of every grievance, including unverified claims
Hold off, and use the frustration to decide properly whether to stay or go

title: Choosing a path for a legacy service hitting its limits
description: A core order service you own has been live for three years and is reaching its performance limit. Monitoring shows QPS already at 80% of the original design limit, and in another quarter or two normal growth will probably overwhelm it. Your manager has given you three months to propose a path, without saying which one. You could rewrite it on a modern framework as a three-to-five-year foundation, refactor it in stages on the current architecture, or ship the smallest performance patches that will carry you through this cycle.

choices.action: Rewrite on a modern framework as a three-to-five-year foundation
Refactor in stages on the current architecture
Ship the smallest performance patches and ride out this cycle

title: A merge conflict wrecks release day
description: The release slips a day. Your manager asks why.

choices.action: Hold a review and add a release checklist
Just say the merge went wrong

title: The company tries to keep you after you look elsewhere
description: You think hard about why you wanted out. Was it money, growth, or a clash with how your manager works? Once that is clear, the question is whether this package fixes the thing you care about. Your manager is sincere and willing to listen.

choices.action: Tell them what is really bothering you, agree a fix, then stay with a clear head
Feel too awkward to be honest, take the rise and leave the real problem unsolved

title: How blunt to be in a code-review comment
description: Priya, who has just joined, opens her first merge request. The design is clearly wrong. You can write in the review that this will blow up in production, or you can ask questions until she sees it herself. The team's culture is fairly direct, and HR has just started talking about psychological safety.

choices.action: Name the problem directly and mark it as must-fix
Use questions so she spots the issue herself
Approve it, and explain on Slack afterwards

title: Do you say the code was AI-generated?
description: You used an AI assistant to generate the core of a complex algorithm, edited it, and opened a pull request. The team has no rule on whether AI contributions need to be flagged. In review a colleague admires how clever the code is — and you realise they have no idea a model wrote the first draft.

choices.action: Note in the PR that it was AI-assisted, and explain what you changed
Say nothing extra, and let it read as ordinary engineering

title: The pay rise did not come through — coast in protest?
description: Your request for a pay rise got nowhere this time. Your manager only said 'let's see'. You feel deflated, and your energy for the work drops. What next?

choices.action: Hold your nerve, keep delivering, build your case for next time, and agree a date to revisit it
Protest by coasting and drag your feet on everything you can
In a huff, tell the whole office 'I'll walk', with no actual plan

title: Do you say the code was AI-generated?
description: Your candour sparks a team discussion about labelling AI-written code. Your manager asks you to lead on drafting a guideline.

choices.action: Take it on and push for a team standard on being open about AI use
Suggest a more experienced colleague lead it, and stay involved

title: Going for a valuable certification that takes months
description: There is a well-regarded certification in the industry that would help your career, but preparing for it would take months of evenings and weekends. The exam fee is not cheap either. You are not sure whether to start now.

choices.action: Set a steady revision plan over several months, broken into daily tasks you can finish
Sign up, then study in fits and starts, and cram at the last minute
Drop the idea because it looks too hard

title: The client praises a feature you did not build
description: In the Cedar Retail project review, the client’s procurement director says: “This real-time stock sync can forecast next week’s bestsellers. That’s ahead of the market.” What you actually shipped is next-day (T+1) batch sync, and forecasting is on next year’s roadmap. Kim, the product manager, catches your eye. Your manager smiles and nods. The review is going smoothly, and about £80,000 of the contract is still waiting to be paid.

choices.action: Say in the room that what is live is next-day sync, and forecasting is a later proposal
Keep quiet in the room and clarify in writing after the meeting
Stay silent and let the review pass

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
description: The team has one place at an industry conference. It is a good trip with plenty of visibility, and word is it will go to you or Jo. Your manager catches you in the kitchen and asks, as if in passing, 'How has Jo been lately? Do you think she's the right person to represent the team?' You can tell they are testing how you compete. The list is due next week.

choices.action: Give Jo fair credit for her strengths and say she would be a good fit
Praise Jo, and briefly add your own recent relevant work
Say you each have strengths, and suggest choosing whoever fits the brief best
Hint at gaps in Jo's recent work

title: You overhear a redundancy list that includes a friend
description: Ethan screenshots your messages about the package. It leaks. You are called into a meeting with compliance.

choices.action: Cooperate and explain exactly how it got out
Deny you told him

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
description: Your manager asks you each to write a one-page case for attending, and a director will decide. You both get to work on it. The atmosphere is awkward but still civil.

choices.action: Keep the one-pager to business value and what you would bring back, without knocking Jo
Compare the two of you in the one-pager and imply you are the better fit

title: Forgetting to water the office plants on your rota
description: Facilities has you on the rota to water the communal plants this week. You got busy and forgot. On Wednesday, Facilities pings you: the plants are almost dead.

choices.action: Water them today and set a calendar reminder
Apologise and ask a colleague to cover this once
Treat it as too small to matter

title: How thorough to be in code review as the team grows
description: Since the team expanded, the weekly review queue has jumped from five or six PRs to more than thirty. As technical owner, you are the named reviewer on most of the critical modules. Each PR now takes 30–40 minutes; one or two hours a day disappear into review. A new colleague's PR is in your queue: the logic is sound, but there are plenty of nits: style, edge cases, naming. You need to decide how detailed this review should be.

choices.action: Review line by line and list every improvement
Focus on core logic and risk, and leave the nits to the author

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
description: The director reads both one-pagers and picks whoever fits the brief better. If you go, Jo will only half accept it. If you don't, you still need to handle it well.

choices.action: If you go, offer to take turns next time. If not, help Jo get ready
Take the win or the loss and put nothing more into the relationship

title: You think the project bonus split is unfair
description: A project closes and bonuses go out. You did most of the work, yet your share is roughly the same as people who barely showed up. The colleague who ran the split clearly favoured some over others. It feels unfair.

choices.action: Raise your actual contribution with whoever ran the split or your manager, and ask for a fairer adjustment
Swallow it, say nothing, and go cold on the project from here
Lose your temper and threaten to coast on the next project, saying nobody should count on you

title: You survive a round of cuts and inherit the work
description: You survive a round of redundancies. Several colleagues are gone, and your manager asks you to cover the urgent part of their work for a short while and to come back with what should wait. Your pay has not changed. Until that conversation happens, you are carrying more. How do you handle it?

choices.action: Prioritise the new work, discuss resources and limits with your manager, and push for support or something in return
Take the lot in silence and carry it at any cost
Push back by coasting: the more that arrives, the more you half-do it

title: How intensely to mentor a new intern
description: An intern, Alex, joined your team this week and, under company policy, is automatically assigned to you as mentor. The first two weeks matter most for onboarding. Alex is sharp but has no domain background and will need a lot of questions answered to get up to speed. Intensive mentoring (an hour of 1:1 a day, reviewing all their code, bringing them into every relevant meeting) would make them independent quickly, but your own output would take a clear hit for those two weeks. A lighter approach (a weekly sync, answering only what they ask) would slow their growth but let you stay on your own work.

choices.action: Mentor intensively so they can work independently within two weeks
Keep a light touch, let them explore, and stay focused on your own work

title: Admitting you are not coping, and asking for help
description: After three months of a high-pressure project you are not sleeping, you cannot concentrate, and your temper is going. Last week you lost it with a colleague in the morning meeting over a design disagreement, and you have been kicking yourself since. The Employee Assistance Programme counsellor suggests a short period of leave. The project is at a critical milestone, and your manager hints that anyone who takes sick leave now can forget a recognition award at year end. Using an award to deter sick leave is poor management. It does not change the notice and evidence the sick-leave procedure actually requires. What do you do?

choices.action: Follow the sick-leave procedure, and privately agree the support and return-to-work plan you need
Grit it out, try exercise and meditation, and deal with it after the project

title: Annual bonus cut and paid in instalments
description: The company announces that the annual bonus, which your contract describes as discretionary, is being reduced and paid over several quarters, citing 'cash-flow management'. A contractual sum could not be cut like this without your agreement. As it is, your expected pay takes a hit, and the move says something about how the business is doing.

choices.action: Take it as a warning: look hard at the company's prospects and adjust your own plans
Complain in public and lead the moaning
Tell yourself at least they are still paying it, and try not to think about it

title: The new manager from outside wants you to inform on the team
description: The manager hired from outside wants a quick picture of the team and takes you aside: 'You've been here. Tell me how people really are and who has issues. I'll remember you for it.' It could be a chance to be useful. It could also be a trap that makes you the informant.

choices.action: Give a fair picture of the team and the work, without informing on anyone or running them down
Embellish complaints about colleagues to please the new manager
Refuse outright and brusquely, even to give a normal briefing

title: You survive a round of cuts and inherit the work
description: You go through the extra work with your manager: what you can carry, what needs more people or time, and why covering at this level should come with something in return. They like how organised you are and that you have taken it on, give you some support, and note your contribution. Covering becomes a way to prove your value.

choices.action: Cover the critical work well, and turn “stepping up” into a case for promotion and a rise
Ease off after the conversation, and do not deliver what you promised

title: Your manager gives you a rise — with a lot more work attached
description: Your manager offers you a rise, then adds, 'Now that the pay is up, you can take on these extra bits of the business as well.' The increase is real, and so is the extra load. The two may not balance.

choices.action: Weigh the extra work against the increase, take what is fair, and say so if it would overload you
Get carried away by the rise and accept every new piece of work without counting the load
Take the rise but quietly dodge the extra work

title: A dependent team is late — do you escalate in the open?
description: A critical piece of work your project depends on, owned by a sister team, is already two weeks late. Their tech lead says privately they 'need another week' but will not update the official plan. The risk to your project is about to show in an update to senior management. You can keep coordinating quietly, or escalate formally.

choices.action: Escalate the risk to senior leadership and ask for a firm delivery commitment
Keep coordinating privately, give them another week's buffer, and prepare a stopgap

title: An undeclared relationship that looks like a conflict of interest
description: Late at night in the office you catch a department lead in a clearly intimate moment with someone who reports to them — well beyond a normal working relationship. That manager is currently reviewing the report's promotion pack, and has just changed their reporting line 'to develop them more closely'. Policy does not ban workplace relationships, but it does require a conflict-of-interest declaration.

choices.action: Raise it anonymously with HR as a conflict-of-interest risk and ask them to look into it
Say nothing. It is their private life, and you have no hard evidence

title: A dependent team is late — do you escalate in the open?
description: A week later they still have not delivered, and your stopgap cannot fully cover the gap. In the project update your risk warning looks late. A VP asks why you are only saying so now.

choices.action: Own your misjudgement of the risk, and ask for a more formal way of tracking cross-team dependencies
Point to the other team's history of slipping, and stress you could only judge what you could see

title: Admitting you are not coping, and asking for help
description: When you come back, colleagues have covered your work and the plan has been moved around your absence. Meanwhile, someone who gritted it out to the end was admitted to hospital with acute anxiety. You can talk about what happened, or keep the details private.

choices.action: If you want to, talk about the leave, and suggest the team builds a workload and support check into how it works
Keep it quiet, and prove yourself again through delivery

title: Another department’s major incident: do you volunteer?
description: The payments clearing centre had a P0 incident last night: a ledger service, unrelated to Halcyon Tech, is posting rubbish. Platform Engineering owns it, and your Lynx Payments team is not in the firing line. The platform director tags every payments tech lead in the leadership channel: “If you know ledgers, get here.” If you go, you face a week of on-call into the small hours, and your membership-benefits proposal is still due this week.

choices.action: Volunteer for the incident team
Offer two hours of remote Q&A in the channel, but do not join on site
Stay quiet and stick to your own work

title: Another department’s major incident: do you volunteer?
description: It takes seven straight days to restore the ledger. The CEO praises the payments team for showing up. The membership-benefits proposal slips and the client complains.

choices.action: Ask your manager for extra people on the benefits proposal in return
Work late to catch up on the proposal yourself, without asking for anything

title: Your company is acquired and the culture flips
description: A larger company buys yours, and reporting lines, processes and culture all have to fall in line with theirs. Everything you knew is changing. Some people are already leaving, and others are watching anxiously. The new owner’s rules and pace still feel foreign. With this much changing, where do you stand?

choices.action: Learn how the new organisation works and where the openings are, adapt, and find where you still add value
Cling to the old culture, resist the new rules, and keep saying how much better it used to be
Play the chaos, commit to nobody, and wait to see who wins

title: In-house kernel versus an open-source stack
description: Two months into the in-house build you are badly behind and keep missing milestones. At the quarterly review your manager puts you on the spot in front of everyone: 'This was your call. The business can't wait. Project X's core modules are already close to your design. Have a look at them, hit the milestone, and nobody's going to diff the code.' It is a way out, though not a clean one.

choices.action: Quietly borrow the open-source kernel, rebrand it, and hit the milestone
Keep the work original, ask for a delay, and write the risk into the update

title: A dinner that is really a fishing trip for team gossip
description: Sonya in Finance, who you barely speak to, takes you to dinner. After the third drink she starts: “I hear Lynx might be merged? Will your manager change? Who on your team might leave?” Her husband is a recruiter and posts on LinkedIn. What you actually know: there is a draft merger plan, not yet decided, and Leo may be moved. None of it is public.

choices.action: Say you do not know, every time, and change the subject
Keep to what is public, but hint that the team may change
Tell her about the draft merger plan and that Leo may be moved

title: Who picks up the bill at a client lunch
description: You have taken a client out for a work lunch. As it winds down they say, "Let me get this," and make a move for the bill. This is ordinary client entertaining, so your side is meant to pay. How do you handle the moment?

choices.action: Having already paid quietly at the desk, say, "This one's on us. You can host next time"
Wrestle over the bill at the table until it gets awkward
Go along with it and let the client pay

title: Your company is acquired and the culture flips
description: You learn the new rules, find the people who matter on the buyer’s side, and come across as open and capable, so they mark you down as someone they can rely on during the integration. They offer you a piece of cross-team work, which means acting as a bridge between two cultures. That is not easy.

choices.action: Take the bridging role, get both sides working together, and build credibility with both companies
Duck the responsibility and push the cross-team work onto someone else

title: Team morale is on the floor — should you step up?
description: After the turmoil, the team is scattered and morale is low. Nobody has much energy for the work, and the gloom is spreading. You are not the manager, but your attitude still rubs off on the people around you.

choices.action: Keep up your own pace, and privately give nearby colleagues some encouragement and a calmer view of things
Join the gloom, pile into the complaining, and make the pessimism louder
Treat it as none of your business, look after yourself, and ignore the team's mood

title: Your manager blames 'the climate' to keep your increase down
description: In the pay-review conversation you name a figure and your manager waves it off: 'The climate is grim this year. The whole company is tightening its belt — that increase isn't realistic.' The wider economy is being used as cover to talk you down.

choices.action: Acknowledge the climate, then bring the conversation back to your actual contribution and market rates
Lose heart at 'the climate' and cut your ask to something tiny
Get heated and snap that the climate is nothing to do with you, and the conversation turns into a row

title: Your first reaction to finding out a newer hire is paid more
description: You find out by accident that a newly hired colleague in the same role, with less experience, is paid more than you. It rankles. What is your first move?

choices.action: Collect yourself, gather your results, and ask your manager for a pay review at the right moment
Start coasting in protest and stop doing the work properly
Complain round the team about how unfair the company is, and spread the discontent

title: You find out a peer got a bigger increase
description: Pay-review outcomes are out. You learn privately that a peer at the same level got a larger increase. It sits badly, and you start to wonder whether you have been short-changed.

choices.action: Compare contributions, find what you can improve, and if needed ask your manager how the assessment was done
Stew in jealousy, take against that colleague, and compete with them behind their back
Ask around what everyone got and spread the comparison to whoever will listen

title: Your annual bonus falls short, and you go to your manager
description: Your annual bonus comes in well below what you expected, after a year of graft and a rating that should have meant more. You are hurt and you have questions. Storm in, or get the facts first?

choices.action: Check your rating, the bonus rules and last year’s figures, then book a conversation about how it was calculated
Storm into the office and demand to know why it is so low
Say nothing to their face, and snipe about the company in the team channel

title: The colleague who buys coffee is collecting favours for a lead vote
description: Harvey brings the team coffees from Pret every day and never takes money. You notice a notebook: “Favours ledger: Chris +2, Ethan +1…” The team is about to pick an acting lead, and Harvey is standing. Today he hands you a larger coffee: “Put in a word for me at the review tonight?”

choices.action: Refuse to campaign. In the review, stick to the facts
Agree to talk him up, in return for later support
Warn your manager privately that someone is trading favours for support
Start buying coffees yourself and join the favours game

title: Christmas at home clashing with the on-call rota
description: You are on the Christmas on-call rota, which clashes with going home for the break. It is the only time in the year your older relatives really get together.

choices.action: Negotiate a fair swap with a colleague, and offer to cover them later
Quietly accept the shift and skip going home
Skip the on-call shift without warning anyone

title: Your annual bonus falls short, and you go to your manager
description: You get the rules straight, then talk it through calmly. Your manager explains this year’s calculation, and along the way you find a place where your contribution really was undervalued. The conversation stays civil. What matters now is what you ask for next.

choices.action: Show with facts what was undervalued, and push for a correction or a catch-up in next year’s rating or pay review
Hear the explanation, feel too awkward to push, and let it go

title: A request to swap on-call over a peak trading bank holiday
description: The bank-holiday on-call rota is out. Owen has a family matter and wants to swap with you. That would put you on cover for the three highest-risk days of the break in a row, during peak trading, when alerts are much more likely. Taking it would really help the team, and Owen would owe you. But three days straight means you cannot leave town, and it will drain you. You could decline and ask your manager to rebalance by the rules. You need to reply in the rota channel tonight.

choices.action: Take the consecutive shifts and cover the three peak-trading days
Decline the swap and ask your manager to rebalance by the rules

title: Colleagues want you to join a group pay demand
description: A few colleagues unhappy with pay have organised and want to go to your manager together to 'push for an across-the-board increase'. They want you in: 'There's strength in numbers — come on.' You worry your manager will treat a group conversation as trouble. That would be his own reading. No rule says so.

choices.action: Back a written case through a staff representative, and do not corner anyone
Decline the group pressure and make your own pay-review case on your contribution
Join in, and block the doorway so your manager cannot leave until you have an answer
Want to join but fear the blowback, so half-agree and then pull out at the last minute

title: Whether to share the method you have kept to yourself
description: The internal tech forum is calling for posts. You have a method for payments circuit breaking and graceful degradation that you have never shared, and it is what makes you hard to replace on the team. Publishing it would probably get a reaction from the CTO and help your promotion case, but colleagues could copy it quickly.

choices.action: Publish the full version and build a personal brand
Post a cut-down version and keep the core parameters back
Don't share it, and keep it to yourself

title: Load-test results clash with what product expected
description: The load test you ran shows the system can only take 60% of the expected QPS. The product owner insists the last demo was fine, so your method must be wrong. The go-live deadline does not move.

choices.action: Invite product to review the scripts and scenarios with you
Stand by the numbers and ask to cut scope or slip the date
Tweak the test parameters until they 'pass', as product asked

title: Anonymous feedback — do you own up?
description: In the quarterly anonymous team survey you left specific suggestions about your manager's style, including some criticism. Afterwards they tell the team that 'anonymous feedback is cowardly — if there's a problem you should say it to my face'. A few days later they take you aside: 'I don't know who it was, but I think you're the most likely to have written those detailed points. I'd like to hear what you actually think.'

choices.action: Own it, walk through the feedback in person, and offer constructive suggestions
Deny it, suggest other possible sources, and protect the anonymity

title: Training a model on customer conversations: where is the line?
description: Product wants a 'smarter support' project: train a large model on old customer-service transcripts. It is technically feasible and could cut human support costs by about 30%. You find that the current privacy notice does not describe this use. Legal says you can sail close to the wind: ship first and update the terms later. That advice is a red flag. A notice does not by itself give permission to train on the data, and stripping out names does not make the data anonymous. The product director promises customers will never know. You are the engineering lead, and the decision is yours.

choices.action: Pause all use of the transcripts until the privacy lead has assessed whether it is allowed, and ship only if so
Train an MVP on public datasets, and run the compliance work in parallel

title: Whether to share the method you have kept to yourself
description: The post takes off. Lauren uses the write-up to improve the system, and your manager asks you to standardise it across the team.

choices.action: Lead training for the whole group and step up as the technical expert
Worry about being replaced and start holding things back again

title: Anonymous feedback — do you own up?
description: Your manager praises you for raising it face to face, then gets defensive about the substance. They explain why those decisions were reasonable, and hint that 'you're only seeing a slice'.

choices.action: Stand by what you observed, admit your view is partial, and suggest more openness about how decisions are made
Ease off, admit you may have lacked some information, and say you still rate their management overall

title: The company asks for a 'voluntary' pay cut to get through a hard patch
description: Leadership asks staff to agree a temporary pay cut to see the company through. Nothing changes unless you agree in writing. They also hint that those who step up first will be remembered. You do not want to look disloyal, and you do not want to give up pay with no prospect of getting it back.

choices.action: Offer to share some of the load if you get a written agreement and a clear route back
Be first to volunteer a steep cut, no questions asked, to look loyal
Refuse publicly and have a go at leadership

title: Training a model on customer conversations: where is the line?
description: Holding the line delays the project by two months. Once live, it works well, but a competitor shipped something similar three months earlier and took the market. At the quarterly review the CEO says compliance matters but cannot be an excuse for falling behind, and there has to be a balance. Afterwards the product director hints that some engineering leads are too conservative.

choices.action: Propose an 'agile compliance' process so the review is quicker next time
Share the case within engineering, and push 'compliance first' harder as an engineering value

title: Load-test results clash with what product expected
description: You find the demo used an ideal path with an extremely high cache-hit rate.

choices.action: Retest and issue a realistic capacity report
Compromise: ship, but with rate limits

title: A job spec from the big tech firm you have always wanted to join
description: You come across a role that closely matches yours at a company you have always wanted to work for. Reading the spec, you feel envious and a bit anxious, because you are not there yet. What do you do with that feeling?

choices.action: Use the spec as a yardstick and close the gaps in your current role until you could get it
Spend the days daydreaming about leaving, refreshing job boards, and letting the day job drift
Envy it and do nothing, telling yourself you would never get there anyway

title: Mentoring an intern as a first taste of management
description: Your manager asks you to mentor a new intern. It will split your attention between teaching, checking in and covering for them, but it is also your first chance to try managing someone. How do you handle it?

choices.action: Mentor them properly: plan, give feedback, and treat it as practice for leading people
Treat it as a distraction from your own work, phone it in and leave them to it
Use them as free labour: odd jobs only, no real teaching

title: Asked where you want to be in five years, you have no answer
description: During a one-to-one your manager asks you seriously: 'Have you thought about who you want to be in five years? Engineering, management, something else?' You realise you have no idea where you are heading in the long term. You are stuck for an answer.

choices.action: Admit you are still working it out, and use the question to think through your long-term direction
Invent an answer that sounds ambitious to get through the meeting, then never think about it again
Shrug it off as a pointless question: 'We'll see as we go'

title: Funding and listing rumours — bet on the share options?
description: Word is the company is raising money or heading for a listing. People talk as if the share options will make them rich, and they tell you to 'hang on a few more years for the options — don't leave'. The rumours are hard to pin down and a payout looks a long way off. You are not sure you should hang a career decision on it.

choices.action: Count the share options as a possible bonus and decide on the fundamentals of the job
Turn down a better offer in front of you and stay put for options that have been over-promised
Ignore the options entirely, count only cash, and leave as soon as something better comes up

title: A milestone briefing for the execs
description: At the company's quarterly leadership review, you have to report on a milestone for a project you own. The execs are short of time and only want conclusions and risks. They have no interest in process. There is still an unresolved risk on the project, and progress is only 'broadly on track'. You have ten minutes.

choices.action: Lead with the conclusion: key results first, then the risk and the plan to deal with it
Give only the good news: hide the risk and stick to highlights throughout
Walk through the process in detail, still not reaching the point ten minutes in

title: Christmas-party rehearsals eating your evenings
description: The department is putting on an optional group number at the Christmas party. The organiser has booked evening rehearsals — an hour or two after work, most weekdays, for a fortnight. Your actual job is busy and your personal plans are a mess. It is voluntary. A lot of people are going, and your manager will notice who does.

choices.action: Show up, and work with the organiser on a tighter rehearsal plan so the day job still fits
Attend every rehearsal and let the day job pile up
Skip a lot of sessions — “I’m not here to dance when there’s real work”

title: A colleague rushed to hospital: a warning for you
description: A colleague around your age, who also works late as a habit, is rushed into hospital. The news hits the team hard. Your stomach drops, because you have been living the same way.

choices.action: Rebuild your sleep and exercise routine, and start actively managing your health
Feel shaken for a bit, then get busy and forget
Use the moment to start a team conversation about cutting pointless overtime

title: Dismissed in a team meeting as "just engineering work"
description: In the weekly team meeting you present this quarter's reliability and performance work. Your manager listens and says, mildly, “This is basically just engineering work. If it runs, that's enough. It won't add much business value. Everyone knows that.” A few colleagues look at their screens and the room goes awkward. You know the work directly underpins the SLA on the core path, and it has real value. You need to decide how to respond in the room.

choices.action: Politely challenge that framing on the spot, with data and business impact
Let it go in the meeting and speak to your manager afterwards
Let it pass in the room, then privately encourage colleagues and spell out what the work achieved

title: A milestone briefing for the execs
description: You opened with the results, then one slide on the risk and the plan already in place. An exec presses: 'What's the worst this risk does? What do you need?' This is a chance to show you have it under control.

choices.action: Answer with a quantified worst case and a clear request for resources
Stay vague with 'shouldn't be too bad', offering no real assessment

title: The new manager quietly moves you out of the inner circle
description: You notice you have been quietly dropped from the core decision-making channel. A few important meetings no longer include you. Nobody has said it out loud.

choices.action: Ask your manager where you stand and what is expected of you
Make your work so solid they cannot ignore you
Nurse the grievance, quietly check out and complain in private

title: Dismissed in a team meeting as "just engineering work"
description: You do not push back in the meeting. Afterwards you take a few colleagues for coffee and spell out the project's value and their part in it, and morale lifts. Your manager does not raise it again, and does not correct the remark in public either. You need to decide whether to take the point further.

choices.action: Use the next meeting's pre-read to put business value in a summary your manager will see
Keep encouraging colleagues privately and do not raise it with your manager again

title: Whether to invest in a CI automation suite
