description: Your team still lacks a proper automated-test CI pipeline. Every release depends on senior engineers manually reviewing critical paths. Your manager wants you to lead the platform work. Headcount has just doubled from five to ten. New joiners' PRs have piled up, review pressure has spiked, and releases are starting to slip. Building a CI suite from scratch, with mocks, load tests and coverage gates, would take about two solid weeks, and two of your scheduled projects would slip in that time. Your manager is not insisting on it, so the call is yours.

choices.action: Spend two weeks building a full CI automation suite
Keep manual review and let new joiners follow the existing process

title: Burnout, and the urge to coast
description: You are exhausted, and one thought keeps coming back: pack it in and just coast. It is a classic sign of burnout, and decisions made on impulse now are the ones people regret. How do you deal with it?

choices.action: Take it seriously: a few days' annual leave, a saner pace, and a workload talk with your manager if needed
Bottle it, pretend you are fine, and keep running on empty
Give in to the urge to coast and start phoning the work in

title: Christmas-party rehearsals eating your evenings
description: You suggest splitting into small-group practice plus a few full run-throughs. It saves a lot of time, people stop staying late every night, and the organiser is grateful. Close to the party they have a family problem and ask whether you can take the last rehearsals and the on-the-night logistics.

choices.action: Step up, run the last rehearsals and the night itself, and get the number on stage cleanly
Decline the lead: “I’ll keep rehearsing, but I’m not running the thing”

title: School run clashing with overtime
description: Your child has just started school. Pick-ups and being there for your child both take time, and this project is busy. At this company, staying late has become the norm, and family time and work are clashing.

choices.action: Share the load at home, agree some flexibility with the team, and make a formal flexible-working request for the school run
Throw yourself into the project and put family time on hold
Try to do everything perfectly at home and at work, and run yourself into the ground

title: Whether to invest in a CI automation suite
description: CI goes live and the team's merge speed improves markedly. New joiners find the configuration harder than expected, though, and the last two PRs sat blocked for hours. A senior colleague suggests loosening the gates so people can get used to the workflow, then tightening them later. You need to decide how strict CI should be.

choices.action: Keep the strict gates and make the team meet the higher bar
Loosen the thresholds so the team can ease into the CI workflow

title: Whether to volunteer as lunch-and-learn speaker
description: The team's lunch-and-learn needs a speaker for the next slot. The topic is callback idempotency, which you have just worked on. Signing up means about 40 minutes of slides, and this week's calendar is already full.

choices.action: Volunteer to speak
Suggest that Priya, who knows this area well, gives the talk
Don't sign up. Stay on delivery

title: The colleague who buys coffee is collecting favours for a lead vote
description: Harvey is named acting lead and puts you on weekend on-call.

choices.action: Take the on-call and keep the relationship
Refuse and draw a line

title: The person next to you wears very strong perfume
description: Your new neighbour wears very heavy perfume. A morning of it has given you a headache. She clearly loves it, and even asks, "Nice, isn't it?" Saying no might hurt her feelings, but putting up with it is miserable.

choices.action: Tell her gently that strong scent gives you headaches, and ask if she could wear less
Praise it insincerely and keep sitting there with a headache
Turn to other colleagues and moan that she "stinks the place out"

title: Seated with a senior leader at the Christmas party
description: The Christmas party seating plan puts you, though you are not senior, on a table with a director you almost never see. A chance like this is rare, and easy to get wrong. After the opening small talk the table goes quiet, and they are looking round the group.

choices.action: Open with something light: an industry anecdote, or an honest take on the evening
Seize the moment and lay the praise on thick so they remember you
Freeze, eat, and say almost nothing all night

title: A side project blurs the line with company business
description: An open-source project you run in your own time unexpectedly takes off and starts to bring in consulting income. It is in the same field as the company but aimed at different customers. You have not used company time or kit. Then a client asks whether you also offer enterprise services, which would compete directly with the company.

choices.action: Tell your manager and compliance now, and ask them to assess the boundary
Decline the enterprise work, keep the side project community-only, and do not tell the company yet

title: The new manager's first team meeting: make an impression?
description: The manager hired from outside is holding their first team meeting, and this is when they start to size everyone up. You wonder whether to push yourself forward and make a good first impression.

choices.action: Come prepared and give a clear, professional update on your work and thinking, without hogging the floor
Talk over people, overstate your role, and put colleagues down to make yourself look good
Keep your head down and say nothing all meeting, terrified of saying the wrong thing

title: A side project blurs the line with company business
description: Compliance confirms you are not currently in breach, but suggests you sign an extra restrictive-covenant clause limiting how far you can take enterprise services later.

choices.action: Accept the terms, so the side project stays within a legal framework
Challenge the extra clause as too broad, and propose a tighter definition of the boundary

title: A metrics problem, ten minutes before the briefing
description: The department’s quarterly review starts in ten minutes. You have just checked the Nebula Growth dashboard. Slide 7 of your manager’s pack says “MAU up 38% month on month”, but that figure mixes trial accounts in with paying users. The external definition counts paying MAU only, which gives +12%. These numbers are the highlight of the briefing. Your manager is making small talk with the VP and asks you, “Pack’s fine, yes?”

choices.action: Quietly point out the definition problem now and suggest correcting it in the room
Hold off for now and email privately after the meeting
Say nothing and let the briefing run

title: Write down what only you know, or keep it in your head?
description: You are the only person who really knows a core product area. For two years you have solved the hard problems, and you have never properly written down what you know. Your manager asks you to run a 'knowledge transfer' session and write a proper design document. You can see that if you hand everything over, you become much easier to replace. If you hold it back, the team carries a risk, and your own career has a lower ceiling.

choices.action: Document it fully: the design thinking, the traps, and a troubleshooting handbook
Write up the basic architecture, but keep the real troubleshooting and deeper principles to pass on in conversation

title: Should you work seriously on management and communication skills?
description: Your technical work is strong, but communication, coordination, and dealing with senior people have always been the weak spots. Whether you stay on the engineering path or move into management, those skills matter more every year. Do you put real effort into closing the gap?

choices.action: Treat soft skills as core skills too: study them and practise them deliberately
Dismiss them: 'the tech is what counts — the rest is fluff'
Say you will work on them, then never practise and keep your head in the code

title: Palpitations after weeks of overtime: whether to stop
description: Two weeks of late nights. Tonight your heart races, your chest feels tight, and your hands shake. These are clear warning signs, but the task is almost done.

choices.action: Stop now, rest, see a doctor if needed, and work at a steadier pace from tomorrow
Drink some water, wait it out, and grind through to the end

title: Seated with a senior leader at the Christmas party
description: Your opener is well judged. The table warms up, they pick up the thread, and they ask in passing what you work on. It is a chance to be noticed, but it is only a passing question, time is short, and this is the wrong setting for a pitch.

choices.action: Say in a couple of sentences what you do and why it matters, then stop without taking over the table
Treat it as a long status update, and sneak in a request while you are at it

title: Health check returning the wrong status
description: Your load-balancer health-check endpoint returns 200, but the body says status is degraded, so traffic still hits unhealthy instances.

choices.action: Fix the endpoint now and check the other services
Fix this service only
Leave it for on-call

title: Write down what only you know, or keep it in your head?
description: The thorough write-up lifts the whole team. Two juniors can now handle problems that used to come only to you. At a promotion review, a panel member says you are technically strong, but it feels as if the team could now cover your current work. Shouldn't you be thinking at a higher level?

choices.action: Take the feedback, and move towards architecture and technical research
Push back: staying deep in the craft still has value, and you will not be 'managed' out of it

title: Where personal use of work kit stops
description: The personal project slows down. Colleagues notice how careful you are, and it quietly counts in your favour in the team. Someone in HR mentions in passing that they are reviewing personal use of kit, and that your approach is worth a look.

choices.action: Join the review and share how you keep work and personal kit separate
Keep your head down. You don't need to preach about a personal choice

title: An engagement survey that asks for your staff ID
description: HR pass on “please set dates more clearly” to Chris. He tries two weeks of stand-ups to fix it.

choices.action: Acknowledge the improvement in the meeting so that it sticks
Wait and see

title: Who owns your side-project algorithm?
description: In your own time, and without directly using company resources, you have built an algorithm related to the company's work. It could be a product in its own right. Your contract says inventions connected to the business belong to the company. That clause alone does not settle it. Ownership depends on your duties, how the work was made, and what the contract can actually do. Being named as inventor is a separate question from who owns the patent. When you share the idea, the patents team ask you to file it as a company patent.

choices.action: Go along with the company filing, but ask to be named as inventor with a personal licence to use it
Argue it is a personal invention with no direct tie to the business, and refuse a company filing

title: A former colleague at a competitor fishes for intel
description: Former colleague Felix has moved to Helios. He once referred you into this job. Over dinner he asks, "Has Lynx locked the team merger yet? What's the Polaris budget?" His contract forbids him from fishing for commercial information from people who still work here.

choices.action: Refuse, and keep the chat to personal matters
Share non-confidential industry gossip
Tell him about the draft merger plan, as a way of repaying the favour

title: A Glassdoor post about the company is doing the rounds
description: A tell-all post about the company is spreading fast on Glassdoor, and only half of it is true. People in the team channel are forwarding it and stirring things up, and they ask what you think.

choices.action: Don't spread it or take sides, and pay attention only to facts that affect you
Forward it eagerly to every chat, adding your own embellishments
Leave an anonymous comment adding more detail

title: Stay deep in the internals, or move to the application layer where results show faster?
description: You face a choice of technical direction: keep digging into hard, slow internals that few people can do, or move towards the application layer, where results show faster and get more attention. Each path has a cost, and the choice will shape your technical standing later.

choices.action: Weigh your strengths, interest, and long-term value, then make a clear-eyed choice
Chase quick wins and easier reviews, and follow the crowd into the application layer
Stay on internals out of snobbery, look down on the application layer, and ignore the practical return

title: A colleague accidentally posts internal architecture online
description: Browsing GitHub, you find that a colleague has posted an architecture diagram of an internal system in a public technical thread. Names have been removed, but anyone who knows the company would recognise it. It is clearly an accident: they were in a hurry to get help with a hard problem. Report it, and they may face disciplinary action. Warn them privately, and you may later be treated as having known and said nothing.

choices.action: Help them take the post down, then report the accidental disclosure to security and say it was a mistake
Message them privately to take it down now, on the understanding that it goes no further

title: At the demo, your manager praises Product and not engineering
description: At the sprint demo, your manager says the product design was excellent and does not mention the late nights engineering put in. The client is on the call.

choices.action: After the demo, email the client (cc'd) with the technical highlights
Jump in on the call to explain how engineering built it
Say nothing

title: Who owns your side-project algorithm?
description: The filing goes through, and you are named as inventor. Being named does not make you the owner of the patent. Once the technical detail is inside the company, your product team folds it into a core product, and the standalone product never gets off the ground. Legal then asks you to agree a separate restriction on related work after you leave. Whether that restriction would hold is a separate question from who owns the invention. Naming a number of months does not by itself make the draft reasonable.

choices.action: Accept it, and put your energy into a new technical direction
Negotiate a waiver of the restrictive covenant, or compensation, for after you leave

title: Balancing a promising idea against delivery pressure
description: You have spotted a new technical approach that could make the system much more efficient, but checking whether it works would take two to three weeks. The current sprint is already full, and your manager is clear that 'delivery commitments are non-negotiable'. You could explore it in your own time, which is slower and leaves you without the team's support, or ask to reshuffle sprint priorities, which would hit this sprint's delivery.

choices.action: Ask for 20% of the sprint to explore, and commit to dropping it if there is no breakthrough in two weeks
Explore in your own time, and only ask for formal resource once you have early results

title: Balancing a promising idea against delivery pressure
description: The request is approved. Some of the team are unhappy: their work is also queued, so why do you get time? Two weeks later the idea is technically viable, but the implementation is more complex than expected and needs more time.

choices.action: Be open about the extra complexity, and ask the team to decide whether it is worth continuing
Promise to finish the implementation yourself, without team time, in return for permission to keep going

title: A colleague accidentally posts internal architecture online
description: Security investigates and judges the leak containable. Your colleague is hurt to find out you reported it, and tells the people they are close to that you shopped them. Helping them take the post down and then reporting the accident was the normal security step.

choices.action: Explain to the team how the report worked, and that security rules are not optional
Say nothing, and trust that time will show you made the right call

title: Dependency upgrade breaks the build
description: Dependabot auto-upgrades a transitive dependency and main goes red. You suspect a breaking patch.

choices.action: Revert immediately, pin the version, and find the cause
Hack the code to match the new version
Disable Dependabot

title: Forced ranking: scoring a colleague who is also a friend
description: It is time for year-end 360 reviews, and the department uses a forced A/B/C split (20% / 60% / 20%). You have to rate Ethan, a friend who has babysat for you and trains with you. But he carried about 30% of the blame for a Lynx Wallet incident this year, and his output has been ordinary. An A for him means taking a slot from someone else. A C could hit his annual bonus.

choices.action: Give him a fair B and write clear points for improvement
Give him an A, taking the slot from a colleague you know less well
Give him a C, because the incident has to show in the rating
Recuse yourself and ask your manager to have someone else rate Ethan

title: The pay-review pot is tight and you are competing for a rise
description: This year’s pay-review pot is small, and too many good people are chasing it. In practice, you and a few equally strong colleagues are competing for the same rise. Your manager’s budget only stretches so far: what one person gets, another does not. If you want that rise, how do you play it?

choices.action: Compete openly on results you can point to and a clear case for your value
Quietly talk a rival down to your manager, so you look better by comparison
Work on your manager personally: a gift, a dinner, a private appeal

title: Colleagues invite you on a self-funded conference trip
description: A few colleagues are planning to go to a tech conference in Singapore over the October half-term, with a couple of visits to friendly companies on the side. Most of it is self-funded. They are keen for you to come and say the trip will change how you see the work. You have a mortgage, and you are not sure the trip will lead to anything.

choices.action: Sign up, but set a budget cap and learning goals first
Stay at home: follow it online and write it up yourself
Dither and leave the message unanswered

title: Forced ranking: scoring a colleague who is also a friend
description: Ethan’s bonus is in the normal range. Privately he says he understands. In calibration your manager uses your comments and asks him to write up the incident.

choices.action: Help Ethan rework the write-up and keep the friendship
Keep your distance and stay strictly professional

title: You notice a remote colleague is often offline
description: While working remotely you notice a colleague you get on with is often offline in working hours, with Slack showing them away for more than three hours, yet their output has not obviously dropped. The team is meant to be outcomes-led, and you also know they are looking after a sick relative.

choices.action: Check in privately: ask how they are, and whether they need help or a change to the arrangement
Leave it and trust that managing by outcomes will sort it out

title: You notice a remote colleague is often offline
description: They admit they are caring for family, and that they are already thinking about leaving. Their exit would leave a hole on a key project.

choices.action: Help them ask your manager for flexible working, and try to keep them in the team
Tell them to decide in their own time, and stay out of it

title: The pay-review pot is tight and you are competing for a rise
description: You make your case with a solid summary of what you have delivered and a plan for what you will contribute next. Your manager accepts that you are capable, but says the others are strong too and there is a balance to strike. Then you hear a rival has been talking you down behind your back.

choices.action: Do not hit back: keep letting your results speak, and set the record straight if needed without attacking them
Get angry, and start talking them down in return

title: An internal transfer into a new area opens up
description: The company has opened internal transfers. You can apply to join a team in a more promising new area. The chance is rare, but you would have to learn a lot from scratch and give up the advantage of work you already know well. What do you do?

choices.action: Weigh your interest and transferable skills, then apply, ready to learn from scratch
Cling to your familiar role and skip the application
Apply on a rush of enthusiasm, without thinking through whether you can close the gap

title: Colleagues invite you on a self-funded conference trip
description: Before you leave, a colleague suggests upgrading the hotel and adding a business visit. That would take you well over your budget cap.

choices.action: Stick to your budget and goals, and skip the upgrade
Say yes to keep in with the group, and worry about the money later

title: Your manager asks: individual contributor or management?
description: You have been in an engineering role for years, and you have reached a crossroads. Your manager sits you down: the company can keep you on the technical-expert track, or move you into leading a team. What do you actually want? This will shape a long stretch of your career, so it deserves a proper answer.

choices.action: Weigh your interests, strengths and the long-term prospects of both paths before you choose
Hear that management pays more and comes with people reporting to you, and pick it without thinking
Dodge the choice and say you are happy either way, whatever the company prefers

title: Asking for remote work or a steadier role for family reasons
description: Your family needs more of you. You are thinking of asking to work remotely or to move to a steadier, less intense role, but you worry it will look like a lack of ambition and hurt your promotion chances.

choices.action: Be clear about the trade-off: make a formal request and commit to keeping your work up to standard
Make a vague request, because you want the easier setup but fear looking unambitious
Say nothing and keep grinding as you are

title: Should you take a transitional role mixing engineering and management?
description: Your manager suggests a transitional role: managing two or three people while keeping part of your engineering work. It would let you test the move from individual contributor towards management with less at stake. It could also mean doing neither job well. Do you take it?

choices.action: Take it as a low-risk trial of management, and plan how you will split your time
Play it safe, refuse any people responsibility, and stay a pure individual contributor
Take it but never split your time, try to do all of both jobs, and fail at both

title: Peer review finds a serious bug in a friend's code
description: Craig, a colleague you get on well with, has an SQL injection risk in his merge request. He messages privately: “Merge it for now — I'll buy dinner tonight and fix it after.”

choices.action: Block the review and require a fix before merge
Merge it and help him fix it this evening
Comment but do not block

title: The promotion only comes if you move into leading people: take it?
description: A promotion is on the table, but the condition is a move into leading people. Pay and level go up, but you would largely leave hands-on engineering behind. It is the fork most engineers reach, where promotion means management. What do you decide?

choices.action: Think through whether you are suited to leading people and actually want it, then decide
Fix on the pay and the title and say yes, regardless of whether it fits
Turn the promotion down without thinking, because change frightens you

title: The office war over windows and heating
description: The temperature in your corner of the open-plan office is a running sore. Hugh always feels hot and throws the windows open as soon as he arrives. Maya always feels cold, so she shuts them and turns the radiator up. It can go back and forth several times a day. Today they snap at each other in front of everyone. Nobody else wants to step in, and everyone looks at you: you are fairly neutral, and people listen to you.

choices.action: Propose a middle temperature, plus a small extra for each: a desk fan, a draught screen
Make the call: set the temperature most people like, and tell them both to stop
Keep your head down and work. It's not your problem

title: Stuck on repetitive work: do you look for something meatier?
description: For a long time your work has been low-value and repetitive. It is steady, but it does not stretch you, and if you stay on it your skills will stall. Do you ask for work with more technical substance, something that would actually make you better?

choices.action: Ask your manager for harder work, or find a way to make the repetitive work itself more efficient
Keep the repetitive work because it is easy and does not take much thinking
Treat the work as beneath you and phone in even the repetitive jobs

title: The office war over windows and heating
description: You set out what each of them needs and suggest a fixed middle temperature, a small screen to keep the draught off Maya, and a desk fan for Hugh. Both feel looked after, and most of the heat goes out of the row. To make it happen, someone has to ask facilities for the extras.

choices.action: Take the lead with facilities and get the extras in
You had the idea. They can chase it themselves

title: Your manager asks: individual contributor or management?
description: You look at yourself honestly. Do you get more from digging into hard technical problems, or from organising people and resources and getting work done through others? Once that is clear, you know which way you lean, and what you would need to build if you took that path. You take the answer back to your manager.

choices.action: Choose the path that fits, list the skills you still need, and ask your manager to help you grow into it
See the answer clearly, then dither and refuse to commit

title: Building a safety net while pay and energy still allow it
description: You realise your career will not always go this well. While your pay and energy are still decent, you start thinking about building a buffer: savings, a second skill or a network.

choices.action: Plan it: build an emergency fund and steadily strengthen one transferable skill
Let anxiety take over: save and study everything at once, and run yourself into the ground
Decide you are overthinking it. Enjoy the present and prepare nothing

title: Grey-area items on a travel expense claim
description: You have just finished a week on a client site and are putting the expenses together. A few items sit in a grey area: 1) coffees you bought the client as a gift (no VAT receipt, only a till slip); 2) a late dinner you ordered for yourself after overtime (policy covers a 'working meal'; late dinners are not spelled out); 3) the taxi to the airport diverted to pick up a colleague travelling with you (about £3 extra).

choices.action: Claim only the flights and hotels, which are clearly within policy, and drop every grey item
Claim as usual, taking colleagues' advice that 'everyone does this, it's fine'

title: Grey-area items on a travel expense claim
description: Finance clears your claim quickly. Colleagues notice the total is well below what people usually claim and rib you over lunch: 'A bit too honest, aren't you? You've left money on the table.'

choices.action: Say it is your own choice, and remind people what the policy actually allows
Smile it off. Keep your own standard without commenting on anyone else's

title: Mentoring a graduate who breaks things
description: The department has taken on a new batch of interns. Your manager gives you Sam, who has the flashiest university and the biggest ego, and hints that mentoring is an unofficial requirement for a top rating this year. You hear Sam nearly caused trouble in another team by merging unreviewed code, and most of the old hands have kept their distance. Do you take on the mentor role?

choices.action: Take it on and set out clearly how the mentoring will work
Decline, citing your current workload

title: Whistleblowing on your manager's fake numbers
description: You stumble on it: your manager has been systematically inflating project numbers in reports to senior leaders, and those numbers are feeding important company decisions. You have solid evidence. Reporting would mean a break with your line manager and an uncertain future. Staying silent could make you look like a party to the fraud, and that could come out at any time. What do you do first?

choices.action: Secure the evidence and report carefully through compliance or internal audit
Speak to your manager privately and give them a chance to put it right
Protect yourself: pretend you did not see it, and keep your distance

title: Emergency hotfix — do you skip the process?
description: Production has a critical fault and needs an immediate hotfix. The standard path of code review, staging checks and a confirmed rollback would take about two hours. A client is in the middle of a live promotional stream, and every minute of downtime is a serious loss. The operations lead hints you could ship now and backfill the process later.

choices.action: Stick to the full process, and turn on a degraded mode to limit the impact on the client
Ship on a shortened path while the team prepares a rollback and completes the review within an hour

title: Mentoring a graduate who breaks things
description: You have been mentoring Sam for barely two weeks when they skip your code review and merge lightly tested code into the pre-production branch. Staging is down all night and several neighbouring teams are blocked. At the next morning's standup your manager asks, stony-faced, 'Who is going to answer for this incident?' Sam stares at the floor. Everyone looks at you.

choices.action: Take the main responsibility and say your oversight as mentor failed
Say in the room that the whole fault is Sam's

title: Emergency hotfix — do you skip the process?
description: The full process takes three hours. The client's live event is badly hit. The sales VP asks openly whether engineering's response time matches what the business needs. The wash-up shows the degraded mode did not fully cover the missing function.

choices.action: In the wash-up, admit the process was too rigid, and propose a graded response for future emergencies
Stress quality first, and point out that a hotfix introducing a new fault would have cost more

title: Whistleblowing on your manager's fake numbers
description: You warn your manager privately first. They deny it, then try to pull you in to 'keep it contained', even hinting it would be 'in your interest to be sensible'. You see they have no plan to stop and want you implicated too. It is messier than you thought.

choices.action: Refuse to join in, keep the evidence, and report through proper channels
Give in to the pressure and inducements, and help cover it up

title: A recruiter rings — do you take the call?
description: A withheld number during work hours: a recruiter, wanting to talk about "a decent opportunity." You are not itching to leave, but it never hurts to know what the market looks like. How do you handle the call?

choices.action: Arrange a time after work to hear them out, without disruption or commitment
Talk it through at your desk, loud enough that colleagues overhear
Hang up and block them, since even talking feels disloyal

title: A promotion without a pay rise
description: Your manager wants to talk about a 'promotion': a bigger title and a heavier workload, with the pay 'held for now — we'll look at it next year'. It is a better title with no rise: more prestige, more work, same money. The question is whether you take it, and on what terms.

choices.action: Weigh what the title is actually worth, and whether it paves the way for a rise, before you negotiate
Get swept up by the title and take the lot without a second thought
Take the missing rise as an insult, refuse on the spot, and leave a sharp remark hanging

title: An intern accidentally emails a rant about the manager
description: Intern Quinn accidentally sends "Chris changes his mind like a rollercoaster" to the whole 200-person department. Two minutes later Quinn is in tears at your desk: "What do I do? I can't recall it." Chris is on the thread and has already read it.

choices.action: Go with Quinn to apologise to Chris in person straight away
Suggest sending a follow-up claiming the account was hacked
Stay out of it and leave Quinn to deal with it
Call IT first and ask whether the email can still be recalled

title: Mentoring a graduate who breaks things
description: You took responsibility in public and Sam is hugely grateful. That afternoon your manager pulls you into a meeting room: 'We're already over our incident quota. Group wants a named person on the accountability report. If you keep this on yourself, the team can't carry it. I suggest you sign the draft that puts the main fault on Sam. I'll try to sort Sam's conversion to permanent another way.' They slide a mostly written template across. Asking for a name to fill a quota is poor management. A fair account of an incident sets out what happened and who did what.

choices.action: Sign the draft and put the main fault on Sam
Rewrite it to match what happened: who skipped review, and which check in the process failed

title: An intern accidentally emails a rant about the manager
description: IT cannot recall it, but they suggest you go and apologise. You take Quinn to see Chris.

choices.action: Go ahead with the apology
Go with the fake-hack story instead

title: How long will the old stack last, and should you switch now?
description: The older technology you have made your living from is still in demand, but the decline is getting harder to ignore. A voice in your head asks: is it too early to move into something new? Would waiting a bit longer be safer?

choices.action: While the demand lasts and you can still think calmly, start learning a new direction now
Tell yourself it will last for years yet, and stay put
Panic and grab at every new direction, dabbling in all of them and finishing none

title: Colleagues invite you on a self-funded conference trip
description: You stay in the UK, follow the talks online and write notes. Someone teases that it does not count if you never left the house.

choices.action: Turn the notes into a team session, and show that staying at home worked
Take the teasing to heart, stop writing notes, and give up on the online talks halfway

title: A promotion without a pay rise
description: You look at it coolly. If the title gives you real experience of leading people or owning a piece of work, and sets up the next pay and promotion conversation, it is worth having. If it is just a vague promise with extra work attached, you should be wary. You take that view into the conversation with your manager.

choices.action: Take on the extra responsibility, but press for a clear pay-review date or the resources to match
Take the title and say nothing at all about money

title: Caffeine dependence and a broken sleep pattern
description: You rely more and more on coffee and energy drinks. They get you through the day, then you cannot sleep, and the cycle repeats. Your focus and mood are both getting worse.

choices.action: Reset: limit caffeine, keep a regular sleep routine and recover gradually
Keep relying on caffeine and finish what is in front of you first

title: Your manager hints that, after this long, you ought to be leading people
description: Your manager needles you, half in jest: 'You're pretty senior on the engineering side — shouldn't you be thinking about leading people, moving up a bit? Staying on the tools forever isn't a plan.' Behind the joke, your manager clearly expects you to make the move soon. How do you answer the hint?

choices.action: Take it as well meant, say whether you'd rather stay technical or try leading, and discuss a plan
Let one remark push you into agreeing to lead people, against what you actually want
Take it as a sign they are writing you off, and snap back

title: A restrictive covenant on the way out: take the pay or keep your options
description: You have decided to leave. When you get to the paperwork, HR produces a new restriction: for a year after you go, you must not join a competitor, in return for a monthly payment. Your better offer is from a company that may or may not count as a competitor. You can read the clause and negotiate, or you can decline it. The company cannot refuse a resignation you are entitled to make. The normal position is that you work the notice in your contract, though you can also agree an earlier leaving date or another arrangement. What do you do first?

choices.action: Read the clauses, take advice if needed, and decide only once you know the scope and payment
Sign cheerfully so the exit goes smoothly, and worry about the next job later
Decline the new restriction outright

title: Share options shrink in a buyback: living with the letdown
description: Years ago you took less cash pay in exchange for share options, and you stayed. A new funding round has cut the valuation hard. HR says the options will be bought back at a very low price. The number that once made your heart leap is now almost nothing. You feel disappointed, angry and misled. What do you do first?

choices.action: Read the scheme and buyback terms, run the numbers and make your case from the paperwork
Take it as your cue to leave and start job-hunting in earnest
Let the grievance show at work: coast, and tell everyone the company over-promised

title: A restrictive covenant on the way out: take the pay or keep your options
description: You work through the clauses: scope, payment, and what happens if you breach. You also weigh the risk that your new employer would count as a competitor. Knowing all that, you can negotiate on equal terms: narrow the scope, raise the payment, or simply go somewhere the restriction does not reach.

choices.action: Negotiate a narrower scope or a better payment, and sign a version both sides can live with
Choose a direction the restriction does not cover and avoid the dispute altogether

title: Share options shrink in a buyback: living with the letdown
description: You go through the option agreement line by line and find that some clauses of the buyback leave room to negotiate. With a few longer-serving colleagues you put a reasoned case. The company softens and offers a compromise: cash, a pay rise, or faster vesting. Now you choose: take something certain, or stay tied in.

choices.action: Push for cash or a pay rise and turn paper value into real money
Trust the company's story again and accept a new option arrangement

title: An undeclared relationship that looks like a conflict of interest
description: Three months later that report is promoted. Other candidates feel the process was unfair and cannot say so. In an exit interview, one of them mentions 'an undeclared conflict in the promotion review'. HR traces it back and asks whether you knew.

choices.action: Admit what you saw, and explain you were not sure at the time whether you should report it
Deny knowing anything. Insist you never saw anything unusual

title: Cost-cutting hits perks — join the complaining?
description: The company is talking about 'efficiency' and has cut some perks, tightened expenses, and shrunk the budget for team socials. The kitchen is full of moaning, and someone starts calling the company tight. You are not thrilled either.

choices.action: Accept the company is under pressure, focus on making yourself more valuable, and stay out of the griping
Lead the public complaining and stir people into having a go at the company
Protest by coasting: the perks have gone, so you do less work

title: Pay-review percentages are out — dwell on the ranking?
description: Somehow everyone's pay-review percentage has been shared around the team, or a colleague has turned the figures into a comparison table. Yours is in the middle, neither top nor bottom. Looking at the table feels a bit awkward.

choices.action: Look once, put it away, and spend your energy getting better so your next review is stronger
Keep staring at the ranking, feel more aggrieved each time, and let it hit your mood and your work
Take the comparison table to your manager and demand an explanation of every difference

title: Pushed to sign a settlement agreement on the spot
description: HR puts a settlement agreement in front of you and wants it signed today. Sign it and you waive claims you might otherwise bring. They say: 'Just get it done — better for everyone.' It is not binding unless you have had time to read it and taken independent legal advice.

choices.action: Ask for time, take independent legal advice, and only sign a settlement you agree with
Sign the settlement today to get it over with, because you are tired of being chased
Lose your temper, tear up the paper and walk out

title: Company-wide AI tools, and the fear of being replaced
description: The company is loudly rolling out AI coding and automation tools, wants everyone using them, and has said that 'the same work will be done with fewer people'. A lot of the day-to-day coding and boilerplate you own is exactly what AI does best. In the kitchen the talk is uneasy: 'Will the next round of cuts be us?' How do you respond?

choices.action: Lean in: learn the AI tools well and use them to get more done
Play along in public but resist in private, sure it will never replace a real engineer
Spiral: spend your energy on redundancy rumours and looking for a safe spot

title: A metrics problem, ten minutes before the briefing
description: Your manager’s face tightens. They drop the slide and go with +12%. The VP asks why it is lower than the figure in last week’s comms. Afterwards your manager says: “Check this a day ahead next time.”

choices.action: Offer to follow up with the VP on how the metric is defined
Leave it there so your manager is not made to look small

title: Whether to volunteer as organiser of the annual team offsite
description: This year's department offsite needs an internal organiser from each team: surveying preferences, choosing the format (outdoors, a meal, board games), liaising with HR and facilities, and hosting on the day. It has nothing to do with OKRs, but it shapes two days for more than eighty people, and it is a chance to show soft skills that managers will notice. Your manager asks in the channel who wants to volunteer. You already have a scheduled project, and this would add an hour or two of offsite prep every day for the next three weeks.

choices.action: Volunteer as organiser
Do not volunteer, and save your energy for the scheduled project

title: Invited to shadow a senior planning meeting
description: As part of your development plan, the CTO invites you to shadow the quarterly executive strategy meeting. In the room you hear sensitive discussion about other departments, including possible restructuring and redundancies in a friend's team. The CTO makes clear it is strictly confidential. Afterwards your friend asks: 'I heard the exec meeting talked about an architecture change. What do you know?'

choices.action: Keep it confidential. Tell them you cannot discuss anything from the meeting
Hint they have reason to pay attention, without specifics, and suggest they talk to their own manager

title: Your partner's job offer in another city: live apart, stay, or rethink
description: Your partner has a strong job offer in another city that could define their career, and taking it would mean living there. You are growing fast at your current company, and your programmes and network are here. The options are living apart, one of you giving way, or making a new plan together. Which way do you lean first?

choices.action: Talk it through, back your partner and look into an internal move or remote working from their city
Keep things as they are: live apart, each build a career, and travel to see each other
Ask your partner to turn the offer down and stay for the household

title: Should you put serious time into an emerging technology?
description: An emerging technology is gathering pace in the industry and looks likely to become mainstream. Learning it properly would take a fair amount of your own time, and it will not help the work on your desk in the short run. Do you learn it, or leave it?

choices.action: Treat it as an investment: make a plan, learn it properly, and look for chances to practise
Skip it as too much hassle and tell yourself you'll pick it up if you ever need it
Bookmark tutorials and sign up for a course so you look like you're learning, but never do the work

title: Company-wide AI tools, and the fear of being replaced
description: You quickly use AI to cut repetitive work by more than half. The time freed lets you take on harder system-design problems. Your manager notices both output and quality rising. Now you face a further choice: stay a highly efficient user, or learn to direct and judge what AI produces.

choices.action: Move up: focus on judgement, design and quality gates that AI cannot replace
Settle for being the fastest pair of hands and stop learning beyond that

title: Invited to shadow a senior planning meeting
description: Your friend feels shut out: 'So you're at a level we don't get to now.' Three months later their team is restructured. They feel they could have prepared if they had known earlier, and the friendship cracks.

choices.action: Explain that confidentiality is a professional duty. You care about them, but you still cannot share
Don't explain. Accept that work relationships sometimes need this distance

title: Your partner's job offer in another city: live apart, stay, or rethink
description: You start living apart, kept together by weekends and video calls. The first months are fine. Then the travel wears you out, you miss important family moments, and the relationship and your energy both start to suffer. One night you race for a late train and turn up to a key review the next day in no fit state. You have to think again.

choices.action: Agree a clear timetable for ending the distance, and plan your career around it
Keep putting off the decision and let things drift

title: A security hole that would be expensive to fix
description: In a routine review you find a potential security hole: under certain conditions, an attacker could reach another user's data. Fixing it means rebuilding the core authorisation module. That touches much of the system, needs a long round of testing, and will probably delay a release that is about to go out. Security rates it medium: fix it soon, but don't block the release. Product is firmly against moving the date, since nobody has complained about it.

choices.action: Block the release until the hole is fully fixed and has passed a security audit
Accept a later fix, but put temporary mitigations and monitoring in first

title: The company wants you full-stack — depth or breadth?
description: The company wants people to go 'full-stack' and be able to pick up anything. Your strength is depth in one area, and now you are being asked to spread out. How you balance depth against breadth will shape what you end up good at.

choices.action: Keep your depth as the base and widen out deliberately, building a T-shaped profile
Learn a bit of everything, master none, and lose the depth you already had
Refuse to widen out, stick to your small patch, and turn down anything new

title: A security hole that would be expensive to fix
description: The release ships on time, and the temporary mitigations hold. Two weeks later monitoring shows access patterns that look like an attack, and the hole may already be in criminal hands. Security responds and confirms that a small amount of customer data was accessed improperly.

choices.action: Open a full incident response: notify every affected customer and report it to the regulator
Scope the real impact, and recommend notifying only customers you can confirm were affected

title: The company goes all-in on a new bet and sidelines your work
description: The company loudly announces it is going all-in on a new technical direction. Headcount, budget and attention all move that way. The work you have spent years on is relabelled 'keep-the-lights-on' and starts to fade. People on the new project look like the future. People on the old product look like a question mark. You are free to say what you think of the technology. Do you try to move across?

choices.action: Push for a place on the new work, start at the edges, and use what you know to catch up fast
Stay put on the old product and wait to see whether the new bet crashes
Spread a story you know is untrue, blame named people, and slow the new team's delivery
Write up the cost, how mature the technology is and the risk of migrating customers, then carry out the decision

title: Build a second curve, or stay focused on the day job?
description: You want a 'second curve' for the longer term: a new technical direction, some open source, or writing up what you know properly. It will take your evenings, and handled badly it could hurt the day job. How do you balance it?

choices.action: Pick a second curve that sits alongside your career, and keep investing without letting the day job slip
Dabble on and off, trying everything and finishing nothing
Dive into the side work and let the day job go to seed

title: The company goes all-in on a new bet and sidelines your work
description: You put your hand up for the new work, start with what you can already do, and contribute quickly on the engineering basics. The people running it notice that you learn fast and can be relied on, and they are willing to give you more. Competition is fierce, though. To stay, you still have to produce something real.

choices.action: Put your head down, make a real contribution and establish yourself on the new work
Get in, then coast because you don't want to keep grafting

title: A database migration window clashes with peak trading
description: You are leading the membership database migration from MySQL 5.7 to 8.0, scheduled for Sunday 02:00–06:00. On Friday, product announces that a peak trading period has been brought forward to Monday midnight. Chris, the DBA, says: 'The rollback script is not fully tested. Going ahead is a big risk.'

choices.action: Ask to delay the migration and protect peak trading first
Cut testing short and go ahead as planned
Propose dual-write with a two-week canary cutover

title: Your idea is pitched first by someone else
description: In a team brainstorm you suggest a design, but it gets little attention. Two weeks later a colleague pitches almost the same idea in a wider meeting, with some of the same wording. A VP likes it and asks them to lead it. You cannot tell whether they got there independently or borrowed yours. Either way, they are now seen as the person who proposed it and will take most of the credit.

choices.action: Speak to them privately afterwards, mention the discussion two weeks ago, and check where the idea came from
Share your earlier thinking with the team, without directly challenging their claim to the idea

title: Your idea is pitched first by someone else
description: Now the team knows the history. People start calling it 'your idea'. The colleague is offended and says in a meeting they understand you had thought in a similar direction, but they developed their proposal independently and took it to delivery.

choices.action: Publicly recognise their independent development and delivery, and make clear you never questioned that
Leave it. Let the team decide who contributed what

title: A database migration window clashes with peak trading
description: Dual-write means building a sync-and-check tool this week, which pushes out a request from the rewards centre.

choices.action: Take it on and ask your manager to drop the other work
Refuse to build the tool, and force a straight choice between delaying and rushing

title: A chatty, skiving colleague eating into your time
description: Luke pauses, says "fair enough", and leaves you alone that day. Over the next few days, though, they tell others at the tea point that "someone has gone rather chilly". You need to decide whether to repair the relationship.

choices.action: Spend ten minutes with them at lunch explaining the boundary and that you mean no ill will
Offer no explanation and keep focusing on the work

title: A former colleague at a competitor fishes for intel
description: InfoSec opens an investigation. Your call records with Felix are pulled.

choices.action: Cooperate with the investigation
Deny it

title: Pitching against a cheaper rival
description: The company is bidding for a major client project, and you are leading the pitch. Your main rival is known for undercutting on price. The panel is a mix of technical people and procurement, so they care about both the solution and the quote. You have heard the rival will almost certainly lead with “we’re cheaper.” How you open will set the tone.

choices.action: Play to your strengths: use technical depth and total cost of ownership to justify the higher price
Slash the price at the last minute to match them, and skate through the actual pitch
Take a swipe at the rival: imply their tech is weak and they have botched jobs before

title: Pitching against a cheaper rival
description: You walk through a solid technical design and a cost-of-ownership model that explains the price. The technical panellists nod along. Procurement still stares at the number: “You’re well above the other bid. How do we sell this to our leadership?”

choices.action: Offer staged payments plus a measurable ROI model procurement can repeat upstairs
Keep talking technology and dodge the pricing question

title: You notice promotions going to the people who play politics
description: Six months on, Harvey is promoted again. You get a tick for "collaboration" and are still behind.

choices.action: Keep working the relationships
Go back to the technical path

title: How thorough to be in code review as the team grows
description: You leave more than thirty comments. The new colleague starts by working through them carefully, but after the third round they message you privately: should they run everything against your bar themselves before opening a PR? Your manager has noticed their PRs are merging more slowly and books a 1:1 to ask how you are reviewing.

choices.action: Turn the standard into a team code-review checklist and roll it out
Go easier on this new colleague until they have found their feet

title: Mentoring a graduate who breaks things
description: After you declined, Sam was given to Chris in the next team. Three months later Chris is seconded elsewhere, and Sam is behind on a client deliverable. Your manager calls you into a meeting room: 'You're the only person in the department who knows this area. You'll have to take over Sam's mentoring and help clear the backlog. There's nobody else.'

choices.action: Take Sam on and help clear the backlog
Refuse again and say you do not have the capacity

title: Dismissed in a team meeting as "just engineering work"
description: Afterwards you book fifteen minutes with your manager and show how the work maps to business metrics. They soften: “Next time, put the business value on page one.” You still sense the rest of the team thinks engineering work does not count. You need to decide whether to fight for the team's visibility.

choices.action: Push to get your work into team OKRs or the quarterly highlights
Keep to your own patch and stop speaking for the team

title: A colleague accidentally posts internal architecture online
description: They are grateful, take the post down, and become more careful about information security. Three months later someone else makes a worse mistake of the same kind: a log snippet containing sensitive customer data, picked up by an external crawler. Security's investigation finds that you knew about the first incident and did not report it, and they question your security awareness.

choices.action: Admit you handled it badly, accept the company's sanction, and propose a 'good-faith warning' route for first minor incidents
Argue that the two incidents differed in severity, and that your call was reasonable in context

title: You bring an outside offer back to negotiate pay
description: You have a real offer from another company, paying more. You are not set on leaving, and would prefer to use it as leverage for the rise you think you are owed here. Bringing an offer into a pay conversation can help or hurt you, depending on how you use it.

choices.action: Be straight: you want to stay, here is what the market pays, and would they review your pay
Use the offer as an ultimatum: “Match this number or I go today”
Inflate the offer and quote your manager a much higher number

title: You bring an outside offer back to negotiate pay
description: You say you want to stay and set out what the market pays. Your manager does not hear it as a threat, takes a proper look, and is willing to fight for a rise, though the process will take some time. You are working on it together.

choices.action: Give them time, be clear about wanting to stay and about your ask, and aim for a deal that suits both sides
Lose patience halfway and switch to a threat

title: After dinner, karaoke with someone on the promotion panel
description: You sing two songs. Helen says you are down to earth. At 1am she asks privately whether you are interested in Polaris — you cannot tell if it is drink talking.

choices.action: Show interest and ask how to prepare for promotion
Talk about the project and leave promotion out, so it does not look transactional

title: Whether to tell your manager about a health problem
description: A follow-up appointment confirms a health problem that needs a course of treatment and will sap your energy. You cannot decide whether to tell your manager. If you say something, you worry you will be treated differently and kept off important work. If you say nothing, you worry about pushing through and dropping the ball.

choices.action: Tell your manager, tactfully, that you need a lighter load for a while and will keep quality up
Tell nobody. Treat it quietly and push through

title: Where personal use of work kit stops
description: Compliance confirm the current use sits inside 'limited personal use', and advise you to 'significantly reduce weekend usage to avoid perception issues'. The written confirmation is reassuring, and it also means the use is now on a formal record.

choices.action: Cut weekend use as advised, and move most of the development onto personal kit in your own time
Keep using it, but avoid commit times colleagues can see, and stay quiet about it

title: A toxic team culture: stay or leave?
description: A newly hired VP is pushing an aggressive 'high-performance' culture: public humiliation for anyone who misses their numbers, briefings that reward stitching colleagues up, and a quiet rank-and-yank. The mood in engineering sours fast, and several people are showing signs of depression. One colleague privately asks you to go to HR together. Another tells you not to stick your neck out, because VPs like this rarely last two years.

choices.action: Join a few senior colleagues in a named letter to HR and the CEO about the culture
Keep your head down, and quietly help people who are being hurt to transfer internally

title: A toxic team culture: stay or leave?
description: You get two colleagues into healthier teams. The VP sees your 'little group' as a clique. In a one-to-one, they say they have heard you are helping people leave the team. If that is your attitude, you might as well join the department you have been sending people to, and free up the headcount for people who want to compete.

choices.action: Take the 'suggestion' and transfer to the team you had already been helping people into
Refuse to be pushed into a transfer, and say you acted out of duty to your colleagues

title: Training a model on customer conversations: where is the line?
description: The MVP is only middling, but Product uses its numbers to argue for wider use of customer data. Then a user asks on social media how an AI seemed to know about their conversation, and a small PR row breaks out. Comms piles in and wants engineering to prove there was no misuse.

choices.action: Pull together the technical records, show the training data was kept separate from the MVP, and recommend starting full compliance now
Back the comms line, lean on the word 'anonymised', and play the risk down

title: An undeclared relationship that looks like a conflict of interest
description: HR opens an investigation and confirms the relationship from other sources. The manager is asked to declare it, denies it, then traces the original report back to you. They start telling the team someone 'went behind their back'. The atmosphere turns suspicious.

choices.action: If confronted, own it and explain you raised a conflict of interest and meant nothing personal by it
Stay anonymous and carry on as normal in the team

title: Desk politics in the new office
description: The department is moving to a new office. Quiet window desks are scarce. Facilities has told teams to sort it out among themselves. Your work needs deep focus and noise easily distracts you, but you also don't want to be known as the person who grabs the good seats.

choices.action: Propose open rules for allocation: the type of work, how often people collaborate, and a rotation
Quietly get a good desk through people you know, and avoid a public row
Don't compete at all, and take whatever desk you are randomly given

title: Desk politics in the new office
description: The first draft of the rules gets a fair hearing. A senior colleague tells you not to be naive: going by length of service would be simpler. The mood in the room turns tense.

choices.action: Compromise: give length of service some weight, but keep rotation and type of work as the priorities
Stick to the original rules and push back on the senior colleague in public

title: Burnt out on the same work: reshape the job or not?
description: You have been doing the same kind of work for a long time. You could do it with your eyes closed, and you cannot find any energy for it. You have stopped growing, the spark has gone, and deep burnout has set in. You can see that if this goes on, you will go stale. Do you reshape the job, or keep numbing your way through it?

choices.action: Work out where the burnout comes from, and design a new direction or a reshaped role for yourself
Keep telling yourself a new job would fix it, and spend your energy on job boards and daydreams
Stay numb, coast, and stall your way through the days

title: Burnt out on the same work: reshape the job or not?
description: You think it through. Is it the lack of challenge, no sense of purpose, or the feeling that you are not learning anything new? Once that is clear, you sketch out changes: automating the repetitive work, taking on a harder brief, or stretching into a neighbouring skill. You take a proposal to your manager.

choices.action: Go after harder work that stretches you, and turn the burnout into a step up
Lose your nerve with the plan in hand, and back off

title: An intern accidentally emails a rant about the manager
description: Chris is silent for ten minutes, then says it must not happen again. Quinn gets a warning and keeps the internship.

choices.action: Help Quinn write a proper wash-up
Step back and stay out

title: A drunk colleague at the Christmas party
description: You keep well clear. Will still unravels in public. Afterwards people know who was near him, who helped, and who vanished. People notice that you treated it as not your problem, and it quietly costs you.

choices.action: Check in afterwards and help him limit the damage
Be glad you stayed out of it, and leave it there

title: A security hole that would be expensive to fix
description: The release slips two weeks. Sales complain about lost deals. At the exec meeting the CEO asks whether a medium-severity issue is worth several million pounds of revenue. The CISO backs you in the meeting, then tells you privately that they held the line this time but want a more balanced answer from you next time.

choices.action: Start a shift-left process, so similar issues are found much earlier
Soften your stance, and promise to be more 'pragmatic' in balancing security against the business

title: Dismissed in a team meeting as "just engineering work"
description: You list SLA gains, a lower incident rate and fewer client complaints. Your manager pauses: “I have seen the data. Time is tight in the meeting. Next time, frame the update in business language.” Someone messages you afterwards: “Glad someone finally said it.” That afternoon your manager calls you in and hints that you should not steal the show in meetings. You need to decide how to carry on.

choices.action: Reframe updates in business language, but keep the technical value in the write-up
Keep speaking up for engineering value in public and accept the political friction

title: Whistleblowing on your manager's fake numbers
description: You put the evidence together carefully and report through compliance under your own name. The company investigates, the inflation is confirmed, and your manager is dealt with. You also become known as the person who reported their boss. Some people respect your honesty, while others are wary of you. Once things settle, how do you carry yourself?

choices.action: Keep delivering solid work so your reputation rests on your ability alone
Talk up the report afterwards and enjoy being the hero whistleblower

title: Empty your savings for a deposit, or keep cash in case work goes wrong
description: After months of looking you have found a flat that fits, but the deposit would almost empty your savings and the family's, and the mortgage would take a large slice of your pay. The industry is uncertain and your product line's prospects are not especially bright. Buying means years of heavy borrowing. Not buying may mean a long wait. What do you decide?

choices.action: Do the sums: pick a mortgage you can live with and keep an emergency cash buffer
Go all in: empty your savings, borrow the maximum and bet your income will only rise
Hold off: build a safety net first and watch how your job and the sector go

title: Empty your savings for a deposit, or keep cash in case work goes wrong
description: You buy a reasonably priced place, keep six months of emergency cash, and the mortgage is manageable. You feel steadier, and at work you can make longer-term choices. Then the company offers a high-risk, high-reward crunch programme. Success would speed up promotion, and failure could drag down six months of performance ratings.

choices.action: With a cash buffer behind you, take the high-reward programme and go for it
Play it safe, take steady work, and pay the mortgage down slowly

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
description: Your manager listens and says, 'Noted.' The list comes out and you are going. Jo takes the day off and is noticeably cooler with you afterwards. When you get back, your manager wants you to give the team a 30-minute talk on the conference.

choices.action: Thank Jo in the talk for her earlier groundwork, then go and speak to her afterwards
Keep the talk on what you got out of it and reinforce your manager's good impression

title: Stuck on the ladder: move into management or go deeper?
description: You are a senior engineer, and you have been stuck at the same level for years. Technical roles above you are scarce, but management posts, oddly, are open. You can keep grinding on the specialist track and wait for one of the few expert roles, or move sideways into management and take a different route up.

choices.action: Look hard at how far each path goes, how well you fit and how the company promotes, before you decide
Push into management, which you neither enjoy nor are good at, just for the title and the pay
Do neither: stay put and complain that the company won't give you a chance

title: Stuck on the ladder: move into management or go deeper?
description: You think both paths through. The specialist track is narrow, but the top of it is valuable. Management is wider, but it is a different job. Weighed against your temperament and how this company works, the choice becomes clearer. Now you have to act on it.

choices.action: Commit: either go for a management role, or go deep enough to gain real technical influence
Finish the analysis but stay on the fence, unwilling to commit

title: A fast-learning new hire stealing the limelight
description: The new joiner is full of energy, picks things up fast, and came in on a lower salary band. They have run a few meetings well. You can feel people comparing them with you in your more senior, more expensive role.

choices.action: Set yourself apart: focus on architecture, quality and the hard problems the new joiner cannot yet handle
Compete on hours and volume to prove you can keep up
Feel sour, quietly freeze them out, and be unhelpful

title: Palpitations after weeks of overtime: whether to stop
description: You finish by pushing through, but the palpitations keep coming back over the next few days. You start to feel rattled.

choices.action: Get checked straight away and make yourself keep a proper sleep routine
Tell yourself you are just tired and keep going round the clock

title: Forced ranking: scoring a colleague who is also a friend
description: The colleague who lost the slot raises it with HR. HR look at the evidence and ask whether you rated him as a favour.

choices.action: Admit the rating was too generous
Insist Ethan deserved an A

title: Communicating a breaking change on a public API
description: Your v3 API drops two v2 fields, which is a breaking change. Of the three downstream teams, one has refused to upgrade for a long time. The contract SLA requires 90 days' notice.

choices.action: Follow the 90-day process and publish a deprecation notice
Privately agree a longer compatibility layer with the reluctant team
Switch v2 off and force them to upgrade

title: Communicating a breaking change on a public API
description: The compatibility layer raises your maintenance cost, and your module's bug rate climbs.

choices.action: Put a sunset date for the compatibility layer into the OKRs
Maintain it indefinitely

title: A former colleague at a competitor fishes for intel
description: Felix pieces the merger together from other sources anyway. Helios goes after your clients with precisely targeted price cuts.

choices.action: Tell compliance you may have overstepped the line
Stay silent

title: Your idea is pitched first by someone else
description: They say they do remember the chat, thought it was just thinking out loud, and had not realised how close it was to what they had in mind. They promise to credit you in later docs. The VP's impression of who proposed it will be hard to undo.

choices.action: Accept the promise. Credit in the docs is enough
Ask them to say at the next update that the idea originally came from you

title: A dependent team is late — do you escalate in the open?
description: Once senior managers are involved, the other team is held to a hard deadline. Their tech lead tells you privately that 'there will be no more informal flexibility after this'. The working atmosphere sours.

choices.action: Go to their tech lead, explain the escalation was about project risk, and try to repair the relationship
Accept the new way of working: formalise every dependency and drop the informal chasing

title: Anonymous feedback — do you own up?
description: Your manager appears to accept the denial, but their expression says otherwise. Later, chances that would have been yours go to other people. The explanation is that 'others need more stretch'.

choices.action: Find a better moment and admit you denied it to protect how anonymous feedback is meant to work
Live with it, let the work speak, and trust time to clear the misunderstanding

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
description: Your manager nods and says no more. Two days later the list is out: Jo is going. She thanks you in front of the team for 'putting in a word'. A week later she shares client leads from the conference, and your manager praises her in the team channel. You have to decide how you feel about it and what to do next.

choices.action: Congratulate her and ask what she got out of it
Congratulate her in public, then tell your manager privately you want the next one

title: Caffeine dependence and a broken sleep pattern
description: Caffeine carries you for a while and you get the work done. Then you keep nodding off during the day and cannot sleep at all at night.

choices.action: Finally cut out caffeine and get back to regular sleeping hours
Increase the dose and keep pushing

title: Lunch with the team, or keep the break to yourself
description: At your third lunch you overhear people discussing who will get places on next quarter’s flagship project. Someone floats your name. Someone else says “we never see them.” You need to decide how often to keep going.

choices.action: Keep lunching with the team every day
Drop back to Tuesdays and Thursdays once you have the key information

title: Invited to shadow a senior planning meeting
description: Your friend over-reads the hint, spreads anxiety through their team, and even starts looking for other jobs. The CTO hears that details of the meeting have leaked and starts tracing the source.

choices.action: Go to the CTO, admit you shared no detail but may have hinted too strongly, and take responsibility
Deny passing anything on, and suggest their anxiety may have come from somewhere else

title: A new manager is hired in, and you start again on trust
description: A new manager is hired in over your team, with a strong background and a style nothing like the last one. They do not know you yet. Some people are already sucking up to them; others are watching coldly. You start from nothing, and they will control your reviews and your prospects. What is your first move?

choices.action: Lead with the work: explain clearly what you are doing and ask what they expect, without grovelling or bristling
Rush to pick their side and lay the flattery on
Watch them coldly, resist, and talk about how much better the last one was

title: A new manager is hired in, and you start again on trust
description: A clear update and solid delivery make a good first impression, and they start taking your views seriously. Then they ask for something the last manager never would. People mutter in private that it is change for change’s sake.

choices.action: Judge the new request on its merits, deliver it well, and add something useful
Join the private muttering that the old way was better

title: Abnormal health-check results: push through or see a doctor
description: The company health-check results are in, and several of yours are flagged: abnormal liver function, a thyroid nodule recommended for further biopsy, and an ECG noting occasional extra beats. The doctor has written, 'See a specialist promptly; avoid late nights and high stress.' These two weeks are the quarterly delivery sprint, and your module is on the critical path. Going for follow-up tests means handing your work to someone else. What do you do?

choices.action: Take leave now for specialist tests and hand over your work cleanly
Push through this delivery and book the follow-up for the end of the month
Decide health checks always scare people, and ignore it

title: A colleague who comes in ill
description: Your manager takes the suggestion and sends Faye home on sick leave. The floor is quieter and people relax. Faye later hears that you raised it and feels a bit hurt, calling it 'a bit ungenerous'. You were thinking of everyone's health, but she never heard that part.

choices.action: Explain privately, ask how she is, and help her hand over what cannot wait
Leave it. You did nothing wrong and there is no need to explain

title: Abnormal health-check results: push through or see a doctor
description: You tell your manager about the results. There is no fuss, and Priya covers for you. Follow-up tests show the nodule is benign and the extra beats are linked to late nights and caffeine. The doctor gives you a plan and stresses sleep. You are relieved, and you also take it as your body's first warning. Back at work, you have to decide how hard to push.

choices.action: Reset how you work: fixed hours, with the high-intensity work spread out
Nothing serious showed up, so you fall back into late-night sprints

title: The lunchtime badminton league and your body's limits
description: The sports club is running a badminton league. The captain wants you in: your game and fitness are both decent. An old neck and shoulder injury has flared up, though, and the project is in a sprint. You want to be part of it, but you know your body has limits.

choices.action: Sign up, and say upfront that the old injury limits how hard you can play
Sit the matches out and help behind the scenes with the draw, the kit and the cheering
Grit your teeth and go all in, to prove you can take it

title: The lunchtime badminton league and your body's limits
description: On match day a teammate pulls out injured. The captain wants you to play an extra game. Your body could manage it, but the risk is clearly higher.

choices.action: Stick to the limit you set, and suggest a substitute
Play the extra game and gamble that the injury won't flare up

title: A database migration window clashes with peak trading
description: Product accepts the delay. Architecture reminds you that 5.7 support ends at the end of the month.

choices.action: Commit to a fixed 72-hour migration plan straight after peak trading
Cite safety and push it back another month

title: An unpublished restructure, and a friend about to buy a flat
description: Sienna does not buy. She tells her husband, who “anonymously” discusses it in an industry group chat. The story reaches HR.

choices.action: Tell HR the truth about how the leak spread
Deny it was you

title: The lunchtime badminton league and your body's limits
description: You run the schedule, the snacks and the group chat so smoothly that the team does well. Someone says it is a shame you did not play.

choices.action: Accept that your role off court still counts, and keep up the support work
Take the bait and jump on court for a game

title: Communicating a breaking change on a public API
description: The reluctant team still stalls, then asks you for more time two weeks before the deadline.

choices.action: Hold the deadline but offer a migration script and support
Slip another 30 days
